TO THE ELECTORS OF THE PJIRLIAMEN- TART DIVISION dF MID-OHESHIRE.
GENTLEMEN,—The accession of your senior member to the Peerage has caused a vr.can2y in the Representa- tion of this Division.
The Council of the Liberal Association of Mid - Cheshire has done me the honour to select me as a fitting candidate, and I consequently venture to ask - for your.suppqrt.,,_, ,

My opinions are so well known to you that I need not trouble you by stating them at any length. I am prepared to give a general and independent support to the present Government, believing IL to be the beat and most Liberal Government that has ever ruled over this kingdom, though I would reerve to myself the liberty, should the occasion arise, of differing from it on the details of any measure.

The programme for the session, as announced in the Queen's Speech, promises much useful legislation. The principles of Local and Municipal Government are to be settled; our Elections are to be made less expensive and more pure, and a Bill to provide legislative com- pensation for unexhausted improvements by the tenant farmer is to be introduced. I am convinced that no Bill on this subject will be adequate that does not contain provision that no tenant should leave his farm without full payment for what he has expended In raising its letting value, and which he has not got back that no sitting tenant should have his rent raised upon his own improvements; and that there shculd be full freedom of sale and culture. / would most earnestly support a Bill containing these provisions, and feel sure that they may be carried out without infringing the rights of the owners of the soil.
I believe also that the present law of agricultural distraint is indefenfrible, and is as injurious to the tradesman as it is oppressive to the occupier.

I should rejoice to see in the Municipal and County Government Bill power given to the representatives of the ratepayers V) deal with the question of licenses. Those who have to pay the bills for the crime, poverty, and lunacy caused by the excessive use of intoxicating liquors, have a right to the control of the number of places where such liquors are sold.

Before the expiration of the present Parliament we are told ti.at Bills to assimilate the County and Borough Franchise, and to redistribute political power will be brought forward. I would give my best sup- post to well considered Bills on these subjeots, and feel sure that they would be passed by a considerable majority of the present House of Commons. But they will require, too, the assent of the House ot Lords, and It is plain that the larger the majority is by which they are carded in the Lower House, the less likely is the House of Lords to resist the expressed mandate of the Nation. I appeal, therefore, to ycu, not to endanger the gift of the Franchise to your less fortu- nate neighbours, by returning as your Representative one who probably would vote against the full gift of the Franchise to the rural ratepayers, or, if he grudgingly assented to the equalised Franchise, would seek by a careful manipulation of botindaries, to make the gift of as small effect as possible.

By the exertions and self-sacrifice of the Viceroy and Chief Secretary, agrarian crime hits diminished in Ire- land, whilst the ameliorating influence of the Land Coutt and of the Ai rears Bill is beginning to have effect, A mutinous conspiracy, such as has from time to time appeared in countries where society is disorgan- ised, has however been brought to light, and has shocked thcse most who had the greatest hopes of the effect of recent legislation. I would urge, however, here and elsewhere, that such crimes are not of the people, but imported among them, and that our policy must still be to act with patience, justice, and sym- pathy.

The beneficent rule. of Lord Ripon in India has re- sulted in such an equalisation of the Balt Duties, as to allow imported salt to compete on fair terms with the native product. I have no doubt but that, when the trade has adjusted itself, the full adoption of the prin- ciples of Free Trade in this article will result in a large increase in our exports of salt, thus conferrineabentfit on the 'Datives of India, as well as IncreAsing the prosperity of our Cheshire salt trade.

I have lived among you now for over 30 years. You have had opportunities of knowing my public and my private life, and in asking you for your votes on this occasion as one who has hitherto tried to serve his fellow-men, I would in all humility, but with confi- dence, appeal to your knowledge of the past as the safest guarantee for my good conduct in the future.
I am, your obedient servant, GEORGE WILLIAM LATHAM.
Bradwall Hall, Bandbach,
February 27th, 1883.

- - THE WRECK OF THE BIRKEFErraps Feb. 28th, 1852. Right on our flank the crimson sun went down, The deep sea rolled around in dark repose, When, like the wild shriek from some captured town, A cry of women roe,. The stout ship Birkenhead lay hard and fast, Caught, without hope, upon a hidden lock; Her timbers thrilled as nerves when through them pawed. The spirit of that shock. Aud ever, like base cowards who leave their ranks In danger's hour, before the rush of steel, Drifted away, disorderly, the planks Front underneath her keel. • Confusion spread; for, though the cosst seemed near, Sharks hovered thick along that white sea-brink; The boats could hold P—not all—and it was clear She was about to sink. "Out with those boats, and let us haste away." Cried one, "era yet yon sea the bark devours The man thus clamouring was, I scarce need say, No officer of ours. We knew our duty better than to care For such loose babblers, and made no reply; Till our goad colonel gave the word, and there Formed us in line—to die There rose no murmur from the ranks, no thought By shameful strength unhoncured life to seek; Our post to quit we were not trained, nor taught To t•-ampl'e down the weak.

So we made Women with their children go. , The oars ply back again, and yet again; 'Whilst, inch by i •ch, the drowning ship sank low, Still under stedfast men. What followed why recall? The brave who died, Died without flinching in the bloody surf, They sleep as well beneath that purple tide As others under turf.

_ They sleep as well; and, roused from their wild grave, Wearing their wounds like stars, shall rise again, Joint-heirs with Christ, because they bled to save - His weak ones, not in vain. • —SIR J. HASTINGS DOLE.

- - A noble part of every true life is to learn to undo what has been wrongly done. "Never say "Bo" to a goose; it is ungrammatical. Say beau to the gander—belle to the g6ose. "Your language is wholly uncalled for," as the publisher told the author whose works failed to sell. ' Our friends often need the perspective so necessary to pictures, in order that they may show to the best advan- tage.—B. M.Prince. A lawyer, attempting to browbeat a female witness, told her she had brass enough to make a saucepan. The woman retorted, " And you have sauce enough to fill Young lady, writing a love-letter for the kitchen-maid: "That's about enough now, isn't it?" Kitchen-maid: "One thing more, miss; just say, please excuse bad spellin' and writin'." A good old Quaker lady, after listening to the extrava- gant yarns of a person as long as her patience would allow, said to him, " Friend, what a pity it is a sin to lie, when it seems so necessary to thy happiness." Life has no smooth roads for any of us; and in the bracing atmosphere of a high aim, the very roughness only stimulates the climber to steadier and steadier steps, till that legend of the rough places fulfils itself at last: "Per aspera ad astra "—over steep ways to the stars.—Bishop Doane. A lady had placed her easel in a field, and sat down by it, sketching from nature, when she was accosted by a boy with—" Please ma'am is that me you're drawing milking that cow in the picture?" "Yes, my little man, bdt I didn't know that you- were looking." "Coz, if it'd me," continued the boy, unmindful of the artist's confusion, "you've put me on the wrong side of the cow, and I'll get kicked." An acquaintance from the country having visited some friends, and being about to depart, presented a little boy; one of the family, with half a crown in the presence .of the mother. "Please is it a good one ?" asked the little fellow. "Of course it is," replied the gentleman, astonished. "Why do you ask ?" "Because I'd rather have a bad one,and then they'll let me keep it. If I get any good money it goes into the bank, and I never get it again.'

• One adequate support For the calamities of mortal life Exists—one only! an assured belief That the procession of our fate, howe'er Sad or disturbed, is ordered by a Being Of infinite benevolence and power; Whose everlastinF purposes embrace All accidents, converting them to good.— Wordsworth. A woman who owned a small millinery shop engaged a painter to paint her a sign. When it came home the other day she savethat it read, " Mrss. J. Blank," (Ix., and she called out, "You have an extra'a' in Mrs.,' and you must paint the sign over again. The painter saw the error, but he didn't want the job of correcting it, and he replied, "Madam, haven't you had two husbands ?" "Yes, sir." You were a Mrs_ when you lost the first?" "I was." a And you think a woman can go on marrying for ever and not lengthen out her title? Mrs! means a marriedwoman or a widow; 'Mrss.' means a woman who has been married twice, and is young enough to marry again; and only yes- terday a rich old chap was in our shop and said if he had any idea that you were heartfree he'd come up—" "Oh, well, you can nail up the sign," she interrupted. And it is there to-day. A Goon MAN'S FALL.—When a good man falls into sin, there are different ways of regarding his transgression. We may sneer at him and his goodness. Or we may experience a shock, and become sad lest religion should turn out to be not altogether what we had been led to believe it. Or we may try to make light of the sin, try to persuade ourselves that because he who has committed the deed is a good man, that therefore his act cannot be so very bad; and thus at- tempt to justify the sinner at the expense of our conscience. But there is another and a more excellent way of viewing the matter. We may approach the whole subject from the standpoint of the mixed character ot human nature. Re- garding no man as perfect, alive to the weaknesses that exist in the best, we shall be prepared to find faults in the lives of the holiest. We shall thus be shocked and grieved at the fall. But we shall not be tempted to make light of it, or to shift it off on that religion which is designed not for "the whole," but for those who, by reason of their sin-tainted nature, require its aid.—The Quiver. THE SPENDTHRIFT CUM.—The Spendthrift Club was so called in ridicule of the very moderate indulgence of its member, whose expenses were limited to fourpence-half- penny each night, yet all of them were wealthy or well-to- • & citizens, many of whom usually met after forenoon church at the Royal Exchange for a walk in the country— their plan being to walk in the direction from whence the wind blew and thus avoid the smoke of the city. "In 1824," says Chambers, "in the recollection of the senior members, some of whom were of 50 years' standing, the house (of meeting) was kept by the widow of a Lieutenant Hamilton of the army, who recollected having attended the theatre in the Tennis Court at Holyrood when the play was the Spanish Friar,' and many of the members of the Union Parliament were present in the house." The meetings of his club were nightly, till reduced to four weekly. Whist was plar4 tor a haTxn. ns .iiPper originally cost only iwt;;nce, and half a bottle of strong ale, with a dram, cost twopence-halfpenny more; a halfpenny to the servant-maid, was a total of fivepence for a night of jollity and good fel- lowship.—Cassell's Old and New Edinburgh. A &ream OF A BANDIT'S CHILD.—Not long ago an old priest was travelling in Italy from one village to another. The priest was glad on looking back to see that a peasant woman, seated in her donkey-cart, was coming that way. Of course the woman asked the priest to take a seat in her call., and of course he very willingly consented. At a turn of the road three robbers sprang out of the thicket. "The Madonna has sent you to us," said one of the rogues, in a pious tone of voice. "Do not fear, worthy father; come down and go with us." It was all very well to say" Do not fear," but the poor priest did fear, and the peasant woman shivered in her sandals. Still there was nothing for It but to obey. After three hours wandering through woods and over mountain-paths, they came to a small open space or plateau, where a group of bandits awaited them, one of whom held a little child in his arms. "Worthy father," said he, approaching the priest and showing him the child, "this is my son, and I wish him to become a Christian. Christen him, or you shall be hanged." You may imagine that the worthy priest made what haste he could to chris- ten the baby. It received a long row of high-sounding names, beginning with Michel Angelo and ending with Guiseppe. When the ceremony was over, the bandit-father presented the priest with a purse of gold, the woman with a pair of costly earrings, and then both were led back to the turn of the road, where the donkey was munching thiettes by the wayside, very much astonished, no doubt, but art Sorry at the delay.—Little Folks Magazine for Mh.

OUR GREAT Grms.—ln September, 1881, we witnessed the test of the 100-ton guns which were about to be sent on service to Gibraltar and Malta. On account of the expense, the test was limited by the War Department to the firing of five rounds; the powder-charge on that occasion con- sisted of 448 lbs. of the most recently approved (powder) pebbles, each about one inch diameter, and systematically arranged in four, cartridges, with means of communication at the end. The projectile was a flat-headed proof shot of 2,000 lbs. weight, or about four-fifths of a ton. The con- cussion is tremendous, but not so hard to be endured as might be supposed, nor so bad as the ring of a brass gun, which sometimes caused blood to start from the men's ears. This gun Is 34 feet in length, and tapers down from 6i feet at the breach to a diameter of 21- feet at the muzzle. The diameter of the bore is 17f inches. The price paid for each of these guns is £16,000; for the manufacture of the pris- matic kind of gunpowder the Government pays one shilling per pound. The total cost of each round is in the aggregate £3O. Some conception may thus be formed of the outlay of treasure which anything like a protracted siege of our, "strong places" will in future involve, and even furnish some political reasoners with a new argument against their retention. Although on the occasion we are referring to One hour was consnmed in firing three rounds, yet with a well-drilled gun detachment it is considered that the opera- tions could be performed in about twenty minates. The projectile used (a proof shot) was fired at a velocity of 1,570 yards, and struck with an energy of 33,500 per foot- tens at the muzzle, so that at a mile range it would destroy three-foot armour. Ther as very little strain upon the gin, the pressure creat by the improved powder being uniformly below 15 tons to he square inch.—The World of el 7Vondsrs. •

div.head: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.
div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

A citizen of Paris claims to have produced, in a new com- pound which he calls panclastite, a means of destruction altogether eclipsing dynamite. Panclastite consists of hypoazotic acid, which is one of the numerous compounds of oxygen and azote or nitrogen, mixed either with essence of petroleum or sulphuret of carbon. The degree of explo- sive force is said to depend upon which of the last-named ingredients is used. • TUE NEW COMET.—A new comet has been discovered by Messrs. Swift and Brooks, two American astronomers. At midnight on the 23rd inst. it was in right ascension 22h. 51m., and north declination 28 deg.; and at midnight on the 24th, the right ascension was 23h. 7m., and declination 30deg. 32m. From these observations it would seem the comet is probably rather bright, as at noon on the 24th it was only half an hour distant from the sun in right ascen- sion. Should this be so, it is likely to be soon observed in Europe, as it is moving eastwards from the sun at the rate of 14 minutes a day. The fact that two observations appear to have been secured, and considerable motion detected, proves that the object is at all events not a nebula. GERMS IN THE BLOOD OF lump ANIMALS.—The venous blood of a horse that recently died of rabies, at Dinan, was examined by M. Barille, with a magnifying power of 1,200 diameters and an immersion objective. It was found to contain an innumerable quantity of small organisms (vibri- ons and bacteria), endowed with motion. The corpuscles, especially the white ones, were profoundly altered; these (white) were much more numerous than usual. Further, there were a number of ovoid corpuscles, about two-thirds or three-fifths of the size of the blood corpuscles, with one to three budding appendices. Haller has described this vegetal ferment of rabid blood, and he calls the fungus Lyssophyton. Lastly, the blood contained a great deal of hemoglobin. OBSERVATIONS ON THE ATMOSPHERE OF VENIIS.—A remarkable proof has lately been given by M. Janssen of the great purity and dryness of the atmosphere on the high desert plateaux of Algeria. •At Mecheria, a military sta- tion there, at which he spent a month, devoting his atten- tion specially to the atmosphere of Venus, he was able to see the satellites of Jupiter with the naked eye; and to apply an eight-inch telescope, magnifying 150 times, to the study of the lunar craters illuminated merely by earthshine, the moon being four days old. Thus favourably placed, and using highly dispersive and perfect spectroscopic apparatus, he is obliged to confess that, relying on spectrum analysis alone, there must be more reserve than has been shown about affirming the presence of aqueous vapour in the at- mosphere of Venus. Any optical evidence of it in the spec- trum is very slight. - ENQLISH ECLIPSE EXPEDITION.—The English expediti- tion to witness the total solar eclipse, of May 6th next 4,„ now ea route for Panama. There are only two obser;ers_ Messrs. Lawrence and Woods, who also formed pa.ll of the expedition to Egypt in May last, when most valuable re- sults were obtained. As it was only fiftc-en days before the latest possible date for departin; that the Treasury sanc- tioned the necessary funds, 'cue preparations had to be made rather hurriedly. B.`.:iore their departure the programme of observations was Arranged, and every second for ten minutes on either side of totality has its allotted work. The opera- tions of the English party will be exclusively photographic, and if the meteorological conditions be favourable over 50 photographs will be taken. Several American and probably some French and Italian observers will also occupy the Caroline Islands, which is the position most favourably situated for observation. A IsTinv COPPER-ZINC ALLOY.—Mr. Alexander Dick, formerly one of the directors of the Phosphor-Bronze Com- pany, has succeeded in producing a new copper-zinc alloy which exhibits characteristics as essentially superior to

1:;;;;;-as-those--of bronze are to gun-metal. The advantages claimed for the new alloy, which has been named "delta metal," are great strength and toughness, and a capacity for being rolled, forged, and drawn. It Can be made as hard as mild steel, and when ,melted is very liquid, producing sound castings of close fine grain. The colour can be varied from that of yellow brass to a rich gun metal; the surface takes a fine polish, and when exposed to the air tarnishes less than brass. These latter characteristics will meet with ready appreciation for cabinet work, harness fitting. ckc. The metal when cast in sand has a breaking strain of 21 to 22 tons per square inch; when rolled or forged hot into rods, the breaking strain is 43 tons per square inch, and when drawn into wire of 22 B.W.G. of 67 tons per square inch.—Engineering. STEAM LAID ON IN PIPES.—We have already shown that steam is especially applicable to heating-purposes under certain conditions; as, for instance in large buildings, or where the heat has to be conveyed distances. It has been applied for warming houses from central depots on a large scale in the United States, upon a plan devised by Mr. Holly. The system is also in operation at Springfield, Mass.; Denver, Col.; Detroit, Mich.; Lynn, Mass.; Auburn, N.Y., and other places. This system appears to have arisen from the advantages accruing to workmen, from having power supplied to them on a combined system. Thus it was found convenient for persons who had steam-engines to combine to obtain steam from one source of supply, and it followed that heat might be conveniently supplied on the line of the steam-pipes. The steam is supplied from a central fire to a large number of houses for domestic pur- poses, and thus the necessity of having separate fires in each house is avoided. In 1880 there were 300 consumers in Lockport, and four miles of pipe. The system had then been in operation four years. The houses are heated from the central supply through about four miles of mains made of ordinary lap-welded wrought-iron steam-pipe, radiating from the boiler-house.—" Our Homes and How to Make them Healthy." • ELECTRIC LIGHTING AND SIGNALLING.—The system of electric lighting with Swan lamps, recently adopted on board the French ironclad le Redoubtable, deserves notice. There are four Gramme machines (of the type of 500 Caredl burners (so-called), each driven by a brotherhood engine. The steam is supplied to each motor by an auxiliary boiler, at a pressure of four atmospheres. Each machine feeds a circuit containing 51 lamps. The first circuit, called the circuit de rade, is meant to work in the roadstead; the second, or circuits de suer, at sea. The machine chamber, lit in the roadstead by 12 lamps in the first circuit, is lit at sea by 37 lamps in the second. The third and fourth ch- culls are called circuit de nuit (night circuits). One of these lights part of the ship where light is indispensable at night; the other chiefly lights officers' cabins, and supple- ments the lighting by the first night circuit. This second night circuit affords, as required, lights for the course (feux de route), and signal lights; the former being six in num,- ber, and equivalent to eighteen of the ordinary lamps used in lighting the ship; the signal lights are ten in number, and equivalent to thirty ordinary lamps. With two commu- tators, one set is exchanged for the other in either case.— Enylish Mechanic. PROFESSOR HUXLEY AND THE RATS.—Professor Huxley

presided on Saturday at the second annual meeting of the London Sanitary Protection Association. In the course of his opening address Professor Huxley said he had made a very great discovery which he wotild make a present of to the members of the assoiciatlon. He had found, in fact, that there was a great body of extremely active and unpaid

sanitary inspectois, to whim he was sufficiently ungrateful to say that he should be glad to hear of their immediate extirpation. These sanitary inspectors were rats. He had had a curious example of their action in his owt ;long, Some time aqo it had been re- -ported. to him that there were rats in a 'Articular rum in the basement. Rats had no place in any London house. The mouse one need not quar- rel with, but rats meant mischief. The rats came from the rats' place, the sewer, and if the rats could come from the sewer all other abominable things could also get up. He had the floor of the room at once taken up, and a very curi- ous state of things had revealed itself. When the house had been built a particular drain of an unimportant character had been designed to lead out in a certain direction. It had afterwards been led in another direction. The business of the builder and his workmen naturally should have been to close up the drain in the one direction which had been finished, and to carry it out in another way. That had been done with a degree of carelessness and neglect of common precaution which was absolutely criminal. The bricklayers had not taken the trouble to shut up a small opening of the drain. For twelve years there had been in the house that connection between the sewer, the drains, and the basement of the house which, had it not been for the rats, would have been impossible to have been discovered, even by the most careful of inspectors.

Sorrows are our best educators. A man can see further through a tear than a telescope. No cloud across the sun, But passes at the last, and gives us back The face of God once more.—Kingsley. That was not bad of an opulent old gentleman, recently deceased, of whom it was asked,"How much did he leave?" "Oh, everything; he took nothing with him." A little girl said to her mother one day, "Mother, I feel nervous." "Nervous I" said the mother. "What is ner- vous?" "Why, it's being in a hurry all over." Unless you honour your life, you cannot get God's best and fullest wisdom; unless you stand upon your feet, you will not hear God speak to you----Phillips Brooks. We all can set our daily deeds to the music of a grateful heart, and seek to round our lives into a hymn—the melody of which will be recognised by all who come in contact With us, and the power of which shall not be evanescent, ike the voice of the singer, but perennial, like the music of the spheres.— W.. 31. Peters, much to the gentleman's distress. Finally, summoning courage, he bashfully .but earnestly remonstrated, "Oh, don't call me Peter's; call me Peet !" " Ah, but I don't know you well enough. Mr. Peters!" said the young lady blushing, as she playfully withdrew behind her fan. Ties LOST Siump.—A curious incident occurred in a large and well-attended church in Clifton one Sunday even- ing. The preacher's subject was the "Lost Sheep," and (luring the sermon it so happened that a real live "lost sheep" strayed from Durdham Down, close by, and got it- self entangled in the iron railings that surround the church. Thus it was that as the preacher made allusion to the "lost sheep" of the parable, the real live sheep at the church door answered, "Bah !" in a very loud but piteous tone. "Which of you," said .the preacher, "having an hundred sheep —" "Bah! bah!" replied the woolly captive out- side. The audience, as it must be at mice perceived, were placed in a position of considerable embarrassment, not to mention the poor preacher, especially when he continued, "For I have found the sheep ;" and the creature at the doer replied, still louder, "Bah !"—Haeper's Magazine. An interesting discussion took place. at Edinburgh last week at the annual meeting of the Scottish Metropolitan Veterinary Medical Association, on 'the use of salt as a pre- ventative of blood and parasitic olseases. Mr. H. Thomson (of Aspatria), Principal Wallcf, Professor Lewis, and other I speakers concurred in reconmending salt as one of the most useful agents for prevent:mg disease. Dr. Morel Mackenz.le has communicated to the British Medical Journal an, account of an outbreak of diphtheria ,at Hendon, which has been traced by him and Dr. Cameron to the infection of the milk supply. Fifteen persons were attacked on a single day. All received their milk from the sami vendor, and no other case occurred among the eom- paratively large number supplied by other dairymen. It has been discovered that the purveyor of the tainted milk washed his cans in water derived from a brook which con- tains a large amount of sewage matter.

THE ADULTERATION OF MILS BY SI7BTRACTION consists of a diminution of the quantity of butter, which may be effected in two ways—by the removal of the cream which is the most obvious way, and also by a practice Which is often carried on by persons ignorant of its fraudulence, that is, the withholding of the "strippings." The latter por- tions of the milk are virtually cream, so that the separa- tion of that portion is equivalent to a removal of the cream, and, if the milk is intended for sale as milk, is just as much adulteration as the other. This practice may account for many cases in which persons have been prosecuted for sell- ing milk deficient in butter, yet have protested most strongly that the milk was never tampered with.. In such cases, if the milk happened to be of poor quality, the with- holding of the strippings for butter-making or household use might be sufficient to throw the butter below the limit, while the sellers might imagine they had done nothing wrong. How TO CUT POTATOES FOR SEED.—If the new doctrine that has been promulgated from the New York Experiment Station concerning the philosophy of potato cutting by single eyes shall prove applicable to ordinary farm practice, there will be a call for a new machine to do the work of cut- ting and planting in a more scientific manner than the cut- feed principle now in use in some of our potato planters. Dr, Sturtevant has been dissecting the potato, and finds it put together something like the o pine tree, the budsne .s,f or eyes of the potato being connected by a BOA of Umbilical cord with the centre ;Ji the potato, at whichpoint is the core or central stem, These internal stems or veins may be plainly st-‹.n in the raw potato by cutting in thin slices from 'stem to seed end, and holding up to the strong light of a lamp. The appearance will be something like the frost- work on our window panes on winter mornings. After the starch grains are bursted by cooking, these veins probably disappear, or are less visible. The new theory is that the potato should be so cut as to keep the connection between the eye and the centre of the tuber. The experiments for the past season showed that an eye cut shallow in every case gave a smaller yield than when it was cut long or deep, so as to reach the centre of the potato. The subject should receive the attention of potato growers the coming season, and, if the new theory proves correct, there will be more care used in cutting seed potatoes in future years. RICE AS FOOD FOR Cerri.n.----" I have used rice meal very extensively for three seasons for my milking cows. I have a large contract for new milk, and keep thirty dairy cows to supply it. The food given them during winter, in addition to hay and turnips, is invariably rice meal and about 21b. decorticated cotton cake each per day. The rice meal is placed, with chopped hay or straw, in a large trough, well mixed up with water, and a good tubful given morning and evening, immediately after milkirtg. My cows have milked very well upon this diet and are in good condition. The milk is remarkably rich, and when churned yields a large amount of butter, though sometimes long in churning. When, on chance occasions, I have been unable to obtain rice meal, and have substituted Indian meal, I have found a diminution in ;the quantity of milk. I cannot find any article that will produce equal results at anything near the price. I pay 13s. for 2401 b., always using the best kind, as I find the second quality very inferior. Some cattle are rather diffident about taking it at first, but soon take to it. I have also used it for fattening beasts, but in such cases mix in oatmeal, as I find the flesh thus is more solid. My horses use it, preferring it to Indian meal. I have also fed pigs with it, and am well satisfied with the results. I begin my young pigs with it, and use nothing else until about the last month, when I substitute oatmeal. My calves, too, are brought up on it. On weaning them from new milk, some rice meal is taken' and scalded and well stirred, to prevent it from becoming lumpy; then it is thinned to the proper state by water, and a little new milk added. Gradually the new milk is taken away, then rice meal porridge becomes their sole diet night Aid morning, with plenty of hay or grass, according to the time of the year. In this way, whilst selling all my-new milk, as nearly as possible, I bring up fifteen to twenty calves annually, and they are in good healthy condition."—"Holleth," in Agricultural Gazette. FOREIGN Burr Ens IN &roma MARKETS.—Mr. T. Higgin, Liverpool, writes to a contemporary, in reply to the state- ment that butter dealers prefer to buy butter from Nor- mandy rather than from the English counties, as follows "I think it is unreasonable to suppose that they have any such preference. As men of business, they no doubt buy wlit thcy can dcal with;t.cct and one can easily under- stand. that they can afford to pay better prices for butter in large parcels of uniform quality—on which no Lime requires to be wasted in tasting, sorting, and selling, or in after disputes and claims—than for small parcels of vary- ing quality, with which they have a great amount of trouble. The experience of the American farmer is that the creamery can get a much better price for its butter than he can obtain for his, and therefore he sends his milk to the creamery for conversion. Professor Alvord, of the Houghton Farm, New Jersey, speaking at Newburgh the other day, showed that the farmers who had made use of the creameries in his State had obtained 3 to 4 cents per pound more for their butter than the farmers who churned their own cream had obtained for theirs, besides the saving of labour; and this is now becoming so well understood that to-day there are ten times as niany creameries in the dairying States of the North-West than there were five years ago. Butter can be better made at a butter manufactory, where cream is dealt with in large quantities and where butter-making is the one business of the establishment, than at a farm, where many other things have to occupy the time and thoughts of the proprietors. The creamery also, sending off its large quantities, can obtain the best rates of carriage by fast trains; for its business is worth the con- sideration of the railroad companies' and it can reach mar- kets 500 or 1,000 miles away, which are quite inaccessible to the individual farmer. It seems to me, therefore, that the establishment of creameries on the co-operative prin- ciple is the remedy for the evils of which your correspon- dent complains; and he would find, I have no doubt, the London dealers quite willing to give as good a price for English creamery butter as they are paying for Normandy butter. The fact for which he vouches, that good English butter is selling in small quantities in country markets at 11d, per pound, whilst Normandy butter in quantity is worth is. sd. per pound in London, only proves that the English butter requires to be got to the London market in a marketable shape, that is in large quantities of uniform quality."

PIGBONS.—THE DRAGOON.-This variety, sometimes called the Dragon, is allied through the Horseman, a now extinct variety, with the Carrier, and is a very beautiful and graceful bird, without the heavy excresences which go so far to mar the appearance of the Carrier. It is a first- rate breeder and [feeder, a good homer, and has many ad- mirers throughout the country. There has, however, been much :difference in the type accepted, the London fancy going in for as much beak wattle as they can possibly obtain, whereas the Birmingham breeders sought for a long, thin held with very little wattle. The latter is to our mind the moi cerrect of the two, but fortunately a compromise" has been made, and there is now a great similarity between the :two styles, and at both London and Birmingham the length of face to centre of eye is li inches, with a mode- rate amount of Jew wattle. The ideal of the shape of beak-wattle is quite different in a Dragoon to that in a Car- rier. The latter is generally convex and arched away from the eye, whereas the former rises behind to its full height and then coming down finer, with the beak like a spike in a "peg-top ;" hence its name, "peg-wattle." In a young bird it is smooth and small, with a line down the middle, but with older birds, as might naturally be expected, it gets rougher and coarser. The eye wattle in a Dragoon should not be larger than a sixpence on a young bird, and perfectly round, but in old birds it seldom preserves this neat appear- ance, and thus the point is an important one. The neck is much shorter than that of a Carrier, and widens at once, gradually to the shoulders. The gullet is clean, and not prominent as in the Owl. The bird does not stand quite so high in the legs as a Carrier, and has a much more compact appearance. Its flight and tail feathers are of more mode- rate length, and one of the great matters is to have the birds with clean and hard plumage. A Dragoon in good condition is a handsome bird, whilst one out of condition is veritably a poor thing. The whole appearance of the head is of the wedge shape, broad at the back and tapering to the front, so that there can be no mistake in this respect as to the difference between the two breeds named. Ihe colours of Dragoons are blue, blue-chequers, grizzles, silvers, whites, yellows and reds, and of all these there are sub- varieties. All have their friends, and there can be no ques- tion that the breed deserved thtf. praise which has been heaped upon it, TRE ;141:1AIIIITIL—STocxmc.-7-In addition to what we uave already said with respect to the-ornamentation of the aquarium, if it be sufficiently large, a very pretty effect may be obtained by making the rock to stand some dis- tance above the water, and leaving a space into which a fern or some other plant may be introduced, the effect of which is very good. Often amphibious creatures, such as newts or small frogs are added to the aquarium, and if this is intenthd a cover must be put over the top, or they will soon be missing, and found where their presence is not de- sirable. In a bell glass tank the cover should be a flat cir- cular sheet of glass, sufficiently large to ptoject an inch over the rim, but it must have a hole in the centre for the admission of air. Of course, where this is done the arrange- ment spoken of in the last paragraph cannot be carried out Newts, and frogs, when kept, must not be always in the water, and upon this account a small floating island should be made. This is done very simply by taking a piece of cork, Smearing it over with marine glue, and then sprink- ling it with sand. When this is perfectly dry, it should be placed in water for some time to season it, and remove all smell, and it will then be ready for use. The creatures for which it is intended will soon testify their approval of. it. Fresh water animals of various kinds are great acquisitions, and really act as the scavengers of the aquarium. They assist in keeping down superabundant vegetation, consume the minute particles which accumulate on the sides of the glass, producing the green film we have already spoken of, and are at the same time most interesting inmates. Of these we may first mention the horny coil shell and the pond mud shell snails, which are to be found in stagnant pools or sluggish rivers, and can be-captured by drawing a net along the submerged stems of rank grass or rushes that grow close to the shore. Then there are two kinds of mussels—the swan and the duck--which can also be used in this way. In addition to these are the water spiders, several varieties of beetles, and the caddis-worm, all of which add to the in- terest of the observer, and at the same time perform neces- sary tasks, which help to make the aquarium more natural and consequently, a greater success. THE SEX OF Culeanfas.—The cock is, as a rule, much larger and more massive than the hen, is bolder and more energetic in its movements, and, in the flight, bustles about in a commanding sort of way, as if anxious to impress the looker-on with the idea that he is the superior animal. Put him in a cage alone for a few minutes, and his carriage is bold and defiant, his chirp clear and ringing, his action quick and decisive and full of fire. The hen is, on the con- trary, smaller and more delicately built, is shorter and more chubby, has a neater head and a softer and quieter eye, is less demonstrative in her movements, and, when put in a cage alone, hops backwards and forwards in a quiet way with a soft, plaintive chirp. The cock, under similar cir- cumstances seems to pull himself together' tightens his feathers, and stretches himself out while the hen is still all over the same hen; she doesn't seem to know why she has been thus isolated, and her demeanour is melancholy rather than fiery and rebellious. Many fanciers of our acquaint- ance can tell a hen immediately by her hop and soft "cheep," or failing that, by her head and eye. We might add that the head of the cock is longer and looks narrower, and experienced breeders can tell the sex of birds in the nest at a glance by this token alone. Possibly much of this may seem to the uninitiated to point to distinctions without a difference; but some of the distinctions are subtle, and such as only experience and accurate observa- tion can determine.

Mica CAGES.—The houses generally used for mice are the ordinary wheel cages similar to those in which squirrels are kept. These, however, we do not approve of, as the mice soon have sore feet, though there can be no question but that they are amusing, especially to children. Fancy cages are not as a rule very suitable, and we prefer to them all plain box ones such as we are about to describe. As these can easily be made by anyone capable of using the most ordinary tools, the question of cost need not be enter- tained at all. For a pair of mice the box should be of the following dimensions :-8 inches long, 6 inches wide, and 3 inches high. The nesting place should occupy one end, and be 2i inches wide, so that it will be 2 inches by 6 inches. The partition between the house and run can be of wood, and have a hole about an inch and a half in diameter, with a small sliding door near one end for the egress of the animals. The top of this nesting place had better be made loose, and in two sections for convenience sake, when any of the inmates are to be caught. A small tin receptacle for food, such:as can be bought at any of the bird shops, will be needed, and can be placed inside here. The run should be covered over with fine wire netting or wire trellis work, and fastened securely, the method adopted in bird cages being as good as any. This it will be as well to have re- movable, but if so, it must not be loose, or the mice will escape. The end of the box opposite to the nesting-place is best made to open as a door, so that the inside can be easily cleaned, and for the same reason we like the outer side of the nesting-place to open also. The best plan is to run a wire down through the side about two inches from one end, and through the floor also, fixed, of course at the top as well, and then this will make a good hinge,the door opening outwards, or it can be hinged in the usual way to the back. A simple button or catch will fasten it when shut, and make it perfectly secure. A larger cage for a buck and half a dozen does would be necessary, and the size would then be 12 inches long, 8 inches wide, and the nesting-place 3 inches wide, but made in two compartments. Larger than this we would not make, but prefer to multiply the number. Show cases can be made with a curvilinear wire top, and ends, back, sides, and bottom to match, but without any nesting- place, but we suppose the cages already described will be sufficient for the majority of our readers. THE STATE OF IRELAND.

THE MURDER CONSPIRACY. John Walsh, one of the prime movers, if not the founder of the Invincible assashaation circle, according to the in- former Carey's evidence, has been apprehended and fully identified at Havre by Deputy-Superintendent Thorpe of Middlesborough. His extradition is expected to follow in due course. Walsh is a man of between forty and fifty , years of age, and unmarried. He worked in his youth as a labourer in Messrs. Bolckow, Vaughan and Co.'s ironworks, Middlesborough, and afterwards at a neighbouring shipyard. He took an active part in Irish movements, and rapidly gained great influence among Irishmen. At the commence- ment of the Fenian agitation, John Walsh became the head centre of the North of England, and so great was the power which bej'acquired that the Roman Catholic Bishop of Mid- dlesborough and other priests sought to discover the respon- sible lead( rs of the movement,but without success. He:was on one occasion denounced from the altarof St. Mary's Church, Middlesborough, and immediately left the church. A very detailed description of " No. 1" is now given by a Dublin correspondent, and the astonishing statement is made that he was in Dublin last week, and is respectably connected and highly esteemed there. He is described as appearing, from his portrait, to be about 45 years of age, and is said to be married and to have a family. He is of Irish birth, but has lived so long in England that he "now talks like his brother cosunercial travellers" in England. A statement by another correspondent is to the effect that he is one Tighe or Tait, formerly a Dublin shopkeeper, and that he will be arrested in the United Kingdom before the lapse of many dap. From the North of England we learn that in several dis- tricts in that part of the country there has been found to exist large organisations connected either directly or indi- rectly with the conspiracy to murder. It is reported that from 5,000 to 6,000 men are enrolled in it, that they have a re- serve fund of fully £5,000, and that they have at least 12,000 revolvers and about 50,000 rounds of ammunition at their command.

From America it is announced that Mr. P. J. Sheridan is still at large, and it is thought probable that the proceedings against him will be abandoned. From Paris we learn that Mr. Bytne is till confined at the Prefecture awaiting the decision of the Government.

From Dublin it is now positively stated that the authori- ties expect to be able to show that several Irish members of Parliament are implicated in the murder conspiracy, but of course no details are given as to the:evidence that will be brought forward against them. Mr. Frank Byrne has, it is reported, been released by the Parisian police unconditionally.

It is stated that Mr. Forster was offered police protection after his recent speech, but dcclined it. The death is reported 31 a bailiff in the employ of Lord Ardilaun, who was badly beaten a few days ago by two strangers, who appear to have waylaid him. It is stated that Mr. Field, the Dublin juror who was at- taaed in the street last November, has lodged a claim for £lO,OOO compensation. The Castlerea constabulary have arrested six men whom they found holding a secret meeting in a public-house. On one of the prisoners, an ex-suspect it is said, a letter from an Irish M.P. was found, to which the police attach much importance. A shocking accident occurred at Ballincollig Barrack, near Cork, on Friday night. The provost-sergeant of the Scots Greys, seeing a man whom he took to be a stranger crossing the barrack yard, seized him. The "stranger," who turned out to be Lieutenant Torrens, happened to be carrying a revolver, and the weapon accidentally exploded. The ball pierced the sergeant's breast, and he fell dead. •

Information has been received by the constabulary at Cahir, that early on Saturday morning 16 men, armed with revolvers and guns, forced an entrance into a farmer's house, near Ballyporeen, and ejected the oocupr; named O'Brien, with his family and servants. Some years ago O'Brien purchased the farm for £4OO, and since then attempts have been made by the relatives of the former owner to obtain possession. The sub-inspector at Cahir has left for the locality.

- In opening the County Meath Assizes on Monday Lord Chief Justice May remarked in his address to the grand jury that the cases to be disposed of—only three or four in number—were of a trifling character, and few considering the extent of the county. There was no case of agrarian character, and a very satisfactory sign of the condition of the county was the reduction of the number of threatening letters from twenty at the corre- sponding period of last year to two at the present assizes. CAREY'S SEAT IN THE COUNCIL DECLARED VACANT.—At a meeting of the Dublin Corporation, on Monday, the Town Clerk read a letter respecting James Carey's admission of being guilty of felonies, and suggesting that the opinion of the Council be taken as to his eligibility to continue a mem- ber of the Council. Mr. Webb moved that as Carey had admitted his guilt of conspiracy to murder he was not a fit person to continue a member of the Council, and that he should therefore be removed from office, and his seat be declared vacant by public posting. He refrained from dis- cussing the matter, as the trial of others was pending. Mr. Dobson seconded the motion, which was agreed to without dissension. Mr. Sexton asked was it. legal. Mr. Gray said the question could be raised in the Queen's Bench. MR. O'KELLY, M.P., AND THE FRENCH POLICE.—A Paris correspondent, writing on Sunday night, says Mr. O'Kelly, M.P., who is here on a visit, has been the object of greater attentions than are altogether agreeable to him. Yesterday he started in a cab from his hotel in the Rue Castiglione, and drove to the office of the Justice, in the , Fanbourg Montmartre, to call on Dr. Climenceau. On the way he became aware that his cab was being followed by another cab, and catne to the conclusion that he was being watched by a detective. On his cab stopping at the door of the Justice office the other cab stopped too. Thereupon Mr. O'Kelly went to the pursuing cab, seized the man inside, charged him with being a moucharcl, and hailed a policeman intending to give him into custody. Policemen are never at hand when wanted, and it was rather unfortunate that one was not present on this occasion, for Mr. O'Kelly would have found that for one.man in a cab to follow another man in another cab is not an offence in France. He greyer, the member for Roscommon is said by the Intransigeant to have thrashed the detective, but the Justice intimates that castigation was merely of a verbal kind. Not finding Dr. Clthnenceau at his office, Mr. O'Kelly went to his house, Rue Montaigne, and to his intense indignation he found that he was dogged by two cabs. Judging from tke tone of the paragraphs in the Intransigeant and Justice the member for Roscommon is very anery for being watched and followed. He would be wise to take things coolly.

Two CLSVEIt MARTINS.—Two martins once built under the roof of a cottage, and just when the eggs were hatched, hot weather caused a crack in the clay of which the neat was made, and the young ones fell to the ground. They were picked up unhurt, placed in a basket, and hung under a window-sill. Here the parents fed them, until all but one could fly. This one was very feeble, and cold east winds were blowing down into the basket. But the clever parent birds set to work, and roofed one side with clay, and filled up the holes, and made the basket snug and warm; then they fed the little helpless bird, and watched it lovingly, until it was strong enough to fly. Were not the old birds wise and good ?—/A9-Peep. LINSEED LOAENGES, solidified linseed tea, laxative and Demulcent, 6d ; postage 2d. Kay Bros, Stockport, and all Phemluta.—Achlt.

div.p: LITERATURE.

Tnie CLASSICS TOR TrtE MiwoNt (By Henry Grey, late secretary to the Stockwell Proprietary Grammar School in union with King's College).—We have previously had oc- casion to speak of the excellence of this 'volume, which is an epitome in English of the works of the principal Greek and Latin authors. We are glad to find it is now published at the low price of one shilling, and is therefore placed within the reach of all possessing a taste for literature. To those who have not had the benefit of a classical education the work is of almost priceless value: .

A KlifT TO ILL TUE WAVERLY NOVELS. This is a pamphlet of 32 pages by the author of "Classics for the Million," sold it is published at the low price of 3d. To the students of these interesting novels the key will be found a great assistance in identifying the various scenes and characters so graphically pourtrayed. Great care seems to have been bestowed on the compilation of the pamphlet, the contents of which may be thoroughly relied upon for their accuracy. ALFRED, A DRAMA FOR YOUNG PEOPLR.—In this little drama the author, "It. P.," has succeeded in bringing out one or two of the chief episodes in the good King Alfred's somewhat romantic history, and that, too, in a manner which will impress themselves on the youthful mind. The production indicates a faithful conception of the dramatist's work, and the latent talents of the author in this direction might be very prctitably developed. The drama has, we believe, been very creditably performed at Cairo-street schools.

THE GIANT THITMBLE-WERD OF THE PRAIRIES.—In the great Arkansas Valley there grows abundantly a very curious kind of weed. It is shaped like a round ball, and varies in size from one foot or less in diameter to five or six feet, some specimens being quite as tall as a man. It grows upon a small stem, which is, however, stout enough to bear the mass till it has ripened and dried, when a puff of wind will blow it over, and snap the slender support. With every gust it will now roll away across the prairie, hounding over bushes and rocks, such is its elasticity and lightness. One can readily imagine that when a strong wind blows, the spectacle of a large number of these tumbling weeds is uncommonly funny. They say in the Western States that a party of English sportsmen once mistook these bounding vegetables for bisons, and were at great pains to bring the "animals" within range of their guns. But "out West" they must have their little joke at the expense of English tourists.—Little Fol.

The senior girls numbered 1,2133; passed 161, satisfied the examiners 531, failed 544, absent 32. FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
A severe earthquake was experienced throughout the island of Cyprus on Monday. By the capsizing of a boat on the Yazoo River 16 lives have been' lost.

A band of brigasuis has been attacked on the Turco-Greek frostier by Greek troops. The chief robber was slain, and his followers driven back into Turkish territory. Four Frenah war vessels have arrived off the north-west coast of Madagascar. Great excitement prevails, and the Malagasy people are preparing to resist the French. In commemoration of the silver wedding of the Crown Prince and Princess of Prussia, it is proposed to erect an English church in Berlin by voluntary subscriptions. There is some probability of a modification of the Egyptian Ministry, and it is anticipated that in any redis= tribution of offices a portfolio may be given to Nubar Pasha.
A Paris telegram states that the spread of the revolu- tionary movement throughout Europe will shortly form the subject of serious negotiations among the leading Powers.
On Sunday a meeting was held at the Lille, at which a resolution in favour of the Royalist cause in France was passed, It is stated that there were about 5,000 persons present.

- A telegram from Teheran states that a body of Saruk Tur- comans have crossed the Harirud River, with the object of attacking the Persian Turcomans. They were repulsed, but it is believed that they intend to make another raid. From next May there will be a "lightning train " be- tween Paris and Vienna, the transit occupying •27 hours; and the journey from Paris to Constantinople will be re- duced from 111 to 78 hours.
The Standard has reason to believe that when the Viceroy of India leaves tor the Hills at the end of the present month an interview will be arranged between him and the Ameer of Afghanistan... _

The Mery Tekke chief, Berdy Abou, whose band attacked the party with the topographer Parfenoff, and killed three Cossacks, has been shot at Askabad. His accomplice was sentenced to hard labour for life.

s.ccording to a Cairo correspondent, six English teachers have been sent to fill the posts in the Government schools. This, he adds, is the first step towards the substitution of English for French as the language of common intercourse among foreigners. The French Government have selected New Caledonia, the New Hebrides, the Loyalty Islands, and the territory of Ankara, a portion of Madagascar subject to French protec- torate, as places to which habitual criminals shall be tran- sported under the Bill now pending. Wednesday being the first anniversary of the proclama- tion of Servia as a kingdom, a grand parade of the troops was held before King Milan' and a Te Ded7ll was sung in the cathedral, at which all the members of the diplomatic body were present. It is announced in the Algerian papers that an expedition is being organised agaiast the renowned chief Bou Amema, who has hitherto eluded all attempts to lay bands on him. Quantities of provisions are being stored in the southern garrisons, and the troops are being trained for long marches.

Further discoveries of an important character have been made in Andalusia, and the Government seem now to be fully acquainted with the constitution and objects of the formidable "Society of the Black Hand." The object of the Association was "to Wage an implacable war against capital." It is stated that M. de Lesseps will start in a few days for Africa to examine the borings effected by Commander 0 udier with a view to the formation of an island sea. If these bor- ings show that it will be necessary to remove stone, the idea will be abandoned; but if only sand would need to be exca- vated, M. de Lesseps asserts that the enterprise will be car- ried out.

CETINVATO.—A te:egram from Durban states that Cate- __ wayo is building three military kraals. A mounted native police, numbering 60 men, under two European officers, has been organised for the protection of the reserved territory. The tribal disturbances in Pondoland still continue. Some alarm has been caused in Griqualand East by a reported collision between the Pondos and Basutos.

President Arthur has signed the New Tariff Bill which Was agreed to at a conference of both Houses at Washington. The Chairman of the Committee of Ways and Means has stated that the new tariff will bring about a reduction of revenue to the amount of 67 millions of dollars. One of the opponents of the Bill pointed out that the reduction on the foreign tariff would only amount to 25 millions of dollars. • The Prince of Wales has received the rank of a Field Marshal in the Prussian Army. The same honour was con- ferred upon the " Iron Duke" after Waterloo, and the Prince's fellow-marshalls now include Count Moltke, the "Red Prince," and two other generals scircely less dis- tinguished—Manteuffel and Bittenfeld. The Times corre- spondent says that the new appointment is "spoken of in military circles with a certain amount of incredulous sur- prise." _

THE DEMOLITION OF THE TUILERIES.—The demolition of the Tuileries does not progress very rapidly, though some eighty men are employed. The palace proves to have been abominably built. Except the facade, the stonework is found, much to the disappointment of the contractor, to whom the materials were sold, to be of the most rubbishy description, and the interior columns, which were supposed to be solid, turn out, it is said, to be mouldings over rough blocks. No object has yet been found more interesting than an old bunch of one hundred keys. A Cairo correspondent says the Indemnity Commission is making good progress, having disposed of over a hundred claims, either for the destruction of buildings or of other property, which were tiled for less than £2OO in each case. Claims for buildings have been given precedence, in the hope that the owners, by rebuilding, will afford employment to mechanics. The correspondent adds that Egypt is threatenea with an exodus of capital, which is likely to prove most serious. The banks are refusing all credits, and all classes, even the natives, seem desirous of realising any saleable property. Petitions are being signed in favour of the English occupation being prolonged as lorg as possible.

A FRENCH CAUSE CELEBEE. - A Paris correspondent writes :—The extraordinary Monasterio case has entered a new phase. I may remind your readers shortly of the facts. Madlle. Fidelia de Monasterio had inherited a large fortune from her father. Her mother having squandered her own means in disastrous speculations, Fidelia generously sup- ported her. Ultimately, however, the daughter desired to go to Chili, where her father's family live. To prevent her doing so, the mother, with the co-operation of two doctors, had her carried off to a lunatic asylum. The affair causing the indignation of the neighbours, the Police Prefecture interfered, and, finding by independent medical evidence that she was not insane, decided to order the release of Madlle. de Monasterio. Before, however, he could do so, the mother and confederates got her out of the asylum and disappeared with her. The police were then set to work to discover their whereabouts, and soon succeeded in finding the mother and her confederates, who were at once taken into custody. The daughter's biding-place, however, remained a mystery. Now she has been found, and the prisoners are to be released; but she is about to take proceedings against them, as well as against the doctors whose wrongful certificates caused her consignment to a madhouse. The case excites great interest.

div.p: The Prince of Wales was on Wednesday night unani- mously re-elected Grand Master of the Freemasons of Eng- land. The brethren elected Mr. J. Derby Alcroft as Grand Treasurer.

AN EXTRAORDINARY HIDING PLACE.—A case at the Shef- field Police Court, on Monday, disclosed a novel way of secreting counterfeit coins. A man was apprehended on a charge of having counterfeit coins in his possession. On his being searched, however, none could be found, until at length a policeman suggested that the prisoner's wooden leg should be unscrewed. This was done, and twelve counter- feit shillings were found between the socket and the injured limb.

The three persons charged with writing and publishing blasphemous libels in the Freethinker were on Monday con- victed, on a second trial. Foote, the editor of the paper, was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment; Ramsey to nine months, and Kemp to three months. The sentence was received with a " storm of yells and hooting " by the friends of the prisoners. An agitation has already been started with the object of memorialising the Home Secretary to advise the immediate commutation of the sentences. CARRIAOE ACCIDEN'T IN LIVERPOOL: A MEDICAL MAN KILLED.—An accident, by which a medical gentleman and his groom were throwsk out of a gig,and the former sustained fatal injury, has happened in Liverpool. As Dr. Ambrose Cecil Hughes, Roscommon-street, was returning home on Friday evening the horse's legs got entangled with an iron hoop belonging to a child. The animal stumbled, and the gig tilting downwards, the groom was thrown out with con- siderable violence on to the road. The horse took alarm, and dashed forward at a great speed. It is supposed Dr. Hughes stooped to gain possession of the reins, which had fallen from the groom's hands, when he also was precipitated with considerable force on to the road, alighting on his head. The wheels of the vehicle passed over his legs. The groom was stunned by the fall, but his injuries were not of a serious nature, and be was able to attend to his duties on Saturday. Dr. llughes had the attendance of three medical men, but death ensued at eight o'clock on Monday evening. The de- ceased was well known in Masonic circles, and had the re- spect of all. As a member of the West Derby Board of Guardians he rendered excellent services, being at all times solicitous for the care and comfort of the needy.

Smith, Heywood', for improvements in looms for weaving; John Smiley Coey and John McArthur, Leeds, for improve- ments in machines for spinning flax and hemp; Alfred Blechynden, Newcastle-upon-Tyne, for electric governors for steam engines or other prime movers, electric governors for steam boilers and improved connections for steam engine governors; Benjamin Hague, Nottingham, for improvements in stitching machines.—List supplied by Geurge Davie'. div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The Queen held a drawing-room at Buckingham Palace On Tuesday afternoon. The Prince of Wales will lay the memorial stone of the Indian Institute at Oxford, on Wednesday, May 2nd. Mr. Findlater, M.P., has been granted leave of absence from Parliament till Easter, owing to family bereavement. It is stated that the Chancellor of the Exchequer will Introduce his Budget on Thursday the sth of April. The Grocers' Company have subscribed £5OO in aid-of the Peterborough Cathedral restoration. The London Gazette of Tuesday announces the appoint- Ulont of Lieut.-iieneral Smith to be one of the Grooms-in- Waiting in ordinary to Her Majes4y. It has been arranged that the bill to legalise marriage With a deceased wife's sister shall be introdeced into the Rouse of Lords about the end of May. Mr. Justice Chitty on Tuesday refused the application by the liquidator in the winding up of the Northern Counties !lank for leave to institute a criminal prosecution against Our of the directors and the 'auditor. On Saturday, a labourer named George Thornhill, em- PloYed at the Proof House, Birmingham, had his brains Mown out. While charging a gun-barrel for testing pur- Poltes the charge exploded and entered his bead. A fire, causing damage to the- extent of about £3,000, oc- curred on Saturday morning at the charcoal iron manufac- rY of Messrs. Harrison,Ainslie, and Company, Backbarrow, Furness. The Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company's station at Broadfield, between Bury and Heywood, was destroyed 13Y fire on Saturday morning. The station was built of wood, mid this accounts for the amount of damage not exceeding

The weather changed with great suddenness on Monday sight, and on Tuesday was keenly wintry. A COLLIERY on FlRE.—Owing to an extensive fire in one of the roadways, the Pelsall Hall Colliery, near Walsall, has been closed, and over 200 persons are thrown out of work. The fire is supposed to be due to spontaneous com- bustion. A largely atteiftlea meeting of Caledonian Railway ser- vants was held at Glasgow on Sunday, and they unani- mously agreed to accept the promises made by the company through their general manager (Mr. Thomson), and to re- turn to their duty . The Grosvenor Gallery was open to the members of the Sunday Society on Sunday, each member having the privi- lege of introducing a friend. DEATH OF A TRAFALGAR VETERAN.—The death is an- nounced of Captain Ward, R.N., of Slingsby, Yorkshire, at the advanced age of ninety-three. Captain Ward was one of the very few surviving officers who took part in the battle of Trafalgar. He was a midshipman on board the Victory, and he accompanied Nelson's remains to England in December, 1805. Five children of a moulder named Jack, residing in Frederick-street, Glasgow, became dangerously ill on Satur- day night after partaking of supper. The opinion of the doctor who attended upon them is that the seizure was caused by some poisonous Substance contained in herrings, of which the children had eaten. The police are inquiring into the affair. Lord Westbury, writing in defence of pigeon shooting, says he is informed on the hest authority that the name of the Princess of Wales has been made use of improperly in this controversy, as she has never stated or authorised the publication of the paragraph which stated that she had de- termined to " boycott " the Hurlington Club until pigeon shooting has been prohitited. The island of Fettle, about 20' miles west of Shetland, and containing 300 inhabitants, has been isolated by continuous storms from the mainland during the whole of this year till Saturday, when a boat managed to reach it with provisions. The people were found to be in a terrible state of destitution, and many of them must have perished but for this timely IneinUr, Mr. Borlase, M.F.Ezt, 17M on Monday ap- pointed president of the Farmers' Alliance for the erem,ii; , year, in succession to Mr. James Howard, M.P. The Duke of Marlborough has become the president, and has the support of the Bishop of Lincoln Lord Chief Justice Coleridge, Lord Shaftesbury, and other influential persons. On Saturday, on the celebration of his 70th birthday, Professor Macfarren, Principal of the Royal Academy of Music, was presented with a cheque for £800; subscribed by old pupils and other friends, the secret being so well kept that, until the close of the speech of Sir Julius Benedict, who presided and made the presentation, Mr. Macfarren had not the slightest notion of the surprise in store for him. THE EDUCATION CODE.—MUSIC SCHEDULE.—The finish- ing touch has just been put to the New Education Code by the issue of the "Instructions as to Examination in Sing- ing." The two competing systems—(2) the tonic-sol-fa, and (2) the staff notations—are treated with absolute equality. The regulations affecting one of the methods come in Part I. of the " Instructions," and those affecting thc other in Part 11., and since the staff notation is by cen- turies the older method, to it has been accorded the first place in the schedule. In all other respects both systems are dealt with on exactly the same terms, and the require- ments year by year prescribed for each are as nearly identi- cal as the circumstances of the case allowed them to be. The instructions end with the following note : " is hoped that at some future time the relation between the tonic sol-fa and the staff notations Will be taught to scholars in Standard V. and upwards ;" and it is further recom- mended in the case of a school where both systems are taught that the tonic sol-fa system should be used in the three lower divisions and the staff notation in the highest. - ASSIZES LED GAOL DELIVERIES—The following is a copy of a letter recently issued by the Home Office: "Whitehall, 28th February, 1883.—Sir,—I am directed by Secretary Sir William Vernon Harcourt to give you notice that in future the commissions issued to the judges of all assizes, both winter and summer, will be in the old form, and will require the judges to deliver the gaols of all prisoners confined therein at the time of holding the assizes. Prisoners, therefore, must be so committed, and recognisances to prosecutors and witnesses so framed, as to ensure their attendance at the assizes if they are held before the querter sessions, wnetuer tue case us (ale trutwe at me sessions or not. The Secretary of State requests that special I attention may be paid to this to prevent the recurrence of I cases which have occurrea lately where prisoners have been committed and prosecutors and witnesses bound over to ap- pear at quarter sessions and assizes have intervened, and the judge has been unable to deal with such prisoners by reason of the absence of such prosecutors and witnesses.—l am, , sir, your obedient servant, A..F. 0. LIDDELL.—The Clerk to the Petty Sessions, Manchester." THE PREMIER.—There were more than usually crowded attendances on Monday night both in the House of Commons and its galleries, the members and visitors being alike anxi- ous to be present on the occasion of Mr. Gladstone's return to Parliamentary life. Outside, in, and near Palace Yard there was also a considerable crowd, who cheered heartily as the right hon, gentleman, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, drove at a quarter to five o'clock in an open carriage from Downing-street to the Rouse of Commons. The Premier, who looks somewhat sunburnt, and is obviously improved in health' was again heartily cheered on making his appearance in the House. He ente-ed from behind the Speaker's chair, and Lord Edmund Fitzmaurice, who was •at the moment answering a question on foreign affairs, had to pause in his remarks until the cheering eubsided and the Premier had taken his accustomed seat. A few minutes before a reception of almost equal cordiality, and equally corning from both sides the House, had greeted Mr. Fawcett, the Postmaster- General, in making his first appearance since his prolonged absence and serious illness. Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany, was among the occupants of the Peers' Gallery, and remained until after Mr. Gladstone's arrival. MR. BRIGHT ON THE. OLTHS QUESTION.—At a recent meeting of the Hebden Bridge Parliamentary Debating Society, when an adjourned debate on the question of per- mitting members to make an affirmation instead of taking the oath, was resumed. the following letter was read :—One Ash, Rochdale, Feb. 1.4, 1883.—Dear sir,—On the question of oaths, probably there is nothing in the New Testament more espec'allst condemned and forbidden than oaths. To those who do not care about the New Testament this fact will be of no weight. The practice of swearing to the truth of anything makes two kinds of truth or truthfulness. If oaths are of any avail, by so much as they make truth more certain, be so much they lessen the value of an ordinary statement, and diminish the probability of its truth. If ignorant persons are not sworn they think they may tell lies with Impunity, and their lying is made tee a large extent blameless in their eyes. I thine oaths and oath taking have done more than any other thins to impair and destroy a regard for truth. If you wish to see the question treated more at large you will find it in an admirable book, " Dymond's Essays on Morality," which ynu may obtain from any bookseller, or from Mr. Harris, 5, Bishopsgate- street, London.—l am, respectfully yours, JOHN BRIGHT.— Mr. W. Pickles, Royd Terrace, Hebden Bridge. 'SHOCKING CASE OF PARRICIDE AT MATLOCK.—A dreadful affair took place on Sundaes at the house of Mr. Merchant, Chesterfield-road, Matlock 'Bridge. It appears that rooms were taken on Tuesday last by the Rev. Julius Benn, Con- gregational minister, and his son William, a young man of about 24 years of age, of 119, Stepney Green, London. On Sunday morning Mrs. Merchant thought the lodgers had overlain themselves, and at about 12 o'clock she took upstairs a cup of tea, and knocked at their bedroom door. She re- ceived a curious reply and left the tea outside. At one o'clock her husband, who had' gone to church, returned home, and she told him she thought something must be wrong. • He went upstairs, and was horrified to find the young man with his throat cut lying against the door., and II the father in bed dead. It is believed that the young man killed his father at about seven o'clock by striking him on the left temple with a piece of earthenware. There was no sign of a struggle. The first blow probably stunned the de- ceased whilst he was asleep, but his head had received several other blows. The young man afterwards attempted his own life by cutting his throat with a penknife. D. Moxon was called in and ordered him to be taken to the Derby Infirmary. Superintendent Sharp telegraphed to the police at Stepney, asking them to break the news to the deceased man's wife and family. From letters found in the house the young man, it appears. has been in a tow state for a considerable time, and he had come to Matlock for his health. He had previously been in an asylum. The doctor believes be will be able to appear before the magis- trates in about three weeks.—The coroner's inquiry into the case resulted on Tuesday in what may be deemed a merely formal verdict of wilful murder. The evidence showed that the unhappy son had not even been discharged as cured from the lunitic asylum in which he was recently confined, but was only en a "probationary term." Tun " FREETIIINKER" CASE.—The Peterborough Town Council have decided to prosecute a local shopkeeper who had exhibited copies of the Freethinker, and had refused to withdraw them from sale, stating that he had been guaran- teed an indemnity by the public. Mr. John Richard Green, who will be remembered in literature as the writer of the history of the English people, died on Wednesday at Mentoae, whither he had gone on account of his health. A publican charged with the offence was fined 10s., and a case was granted for the Queen's Bench. An important communication was on Thursday received by Mr. Alfred Hardaker, of Liverpool, hon. secretary to the Pawnbrokers' Defence Association, from the Hon. A. F. 0. Liddell, permanent secretary to the Home Office who is directed by the Secretary of State to inform Mr. liardaker, in reply to a question, that pawnbrokers will not be dealt with under the provisions of the Stolen Goods Bill, but if necessary an amendment of the Pawnbrokers' Act of 1872 will be introduced. Shortly after half-past six o'clock on Thursday morning, the extensive premises of Messrs. Windsor, cotton spinners, Radney-street, Oldham-road, Manchester, took fire. The building was fireproof, but owing to the intense heat, the iron girders holding the building together fell, completely cutting the structure to the bottom. The fire, notwith- standing the efforts of the whole of the Manchester Fire Brigade, raged for three hours, and the damage must exceed £50,000. BIGAMY.—A cruel case of bigamy was heard at Accring- ton on Wednesday. In January an engine tenter named Woodhouse, married a respectable girl named Taylor, after " coutting " for several months. He made a number of false and extraordinary representations to her, and got possession of several valuable articles. When she was in- formed that Woodhouse had a wife and four children living in the district, Taylor became unconscious, and has remained in a critical state since. Woodhouse was committed for trial.
