THE IRISH LAND LEAGUE FUNDS.—Lady Florence Dixie returns very vigorously to the inquiry as to what has be- come of the various sums subscribed in the Irish National cause. She finds by diligent research that the Fair Trial Fund started in 1879, the Distress Fund started in 1880, the Land League Fund, the Parnell Defence Fund, :and the Ladies' Land League, have acknowledged receipts amount- ing in the aggregate to £27733, and have only accounted for £125,204. She asks very pointedly what has become of the balance of £152,089, adding that all this money is un- accounted for. Mr. Parnell and his friends have no right, she says, to mock the sufferings of the people in the West of Ireland by asking questions in the House of Commons in- stead of administering practical relief. THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.—A fairly steady tone is maintained in the coal trade of this district, and with the pits kept working on an average about five days a week, present supplies are going away. Colder weather has tended to check any falling off in the demand for house fire coal. For the inferior qualities of round coal the demand is only moderate. In the common sorts of engine fuel there is also some pushing, but this is confined to one or two districts. The better sorts meet with a ready sale, and good qualities of slack are scarce with a decided hardening tendency in price, which in some cases has already resulted in advances of about 3d per ton. At the pit mouth the average prices are as under :—Best coal, 9s 6d to lOs ; seconds, Is 61 to Sc; common house fire coal, 6s 6d to 7s; common coal for steam and forge purposes, 5s Od to Os 3d ; burgy, 5s to 15s 3d; with good slack fetching 4s 3d to 4s 6d, and ordinary qualities 3s 6d to 4s per ton. The scarcity of vessels for coasting cargoes, owing to the recent stormy weather, has caused the shipping trade to be very quiet, and low prices have been ruling both at Liverpool and Garston ; steam coal delivered at the above ports being offered at about 7s 6d, and seconds house coal at about 9s per ton. THE BIGGAR BREACH OF PROMISE CASE.—Mr. Biggar's breach of promise case, on Thursday, drew together a larger gathering to the new Court of Queen's Bench than any can that has previously been heard in it. Barristers, law stu- dents, and curious politicians crowded the court from the opening of the case until its close. Mr:' Biggar, as is well known, went to Paris in 1880, and there was introduced to Miss Hyland, a lady about 35 years of age, be Mr. Egan. This was in October or November, and Mr. Biggar seems to have been so greatly impressed by the lady that on the 19th of November, on the way to church, he promised to marry her. He also, it appears, made Miss Hyland several presents, including a gold chain, a locket, and gloves, and stockings, and on one occasion be knelt down and kissed her feet. Mr. Biggar, however, denied that he ever promised to marry the lady, though he might have called her a darling, and if he kissed her; it was only because she liked it. Still, the jury came to the conclusion, after half an hour's considera- tion. that Mr. Biggar had really made a promise of marriage, Rrici his counsel's plea that his medical attendant had advised I him not to marry did not save him from being condemned to pay £4OO damages. William Smith, an errand boy, was at Birmingham, on Thursday, charged wii.h stealing half-a-crown from his master's till. The case created great surprise and amuse- ment from the Met, according to the police, that the youth was the captain of a youthful secret society. In the "con- spirator's" pocket was found a document containing in his own handwriting the treasonable oath of the society, which was called the " Starlightrider." The oath was as follows :—" I swear that nothing I should hear or see will I divulge, and will do whatever the captain tells me to do or whatever duty he sets me." This document was signed by W. Hazelwood, a youth to whom it was administered, and undersigned by the prisoner "W. C. Smith, captain; and C. Bennett, lieu- tenant." Further statements in the document showed that persons joining the society were to obey the lieutenant in the absence of the captain. There was also a scale of fines for not obeying, for swearing, wed for not attending the secret meetings of the " Invincibles." The. stipendiary, who was considerably amused on reading the document, did not think it a case about which to consult the Home Office —(laughter)—and allowed the youthful "Number One" to be taken home by his father. REPLY TO THE ADDRESS.—Lord Kensington., the Comp- troller of the Household, brought up the usual formal reply of the Queen to the address. Trim EGYPTIAN Vovßs.—The House then went into Com- mittee oi discussed the Egyptian vote.—ln re- plying to several questions on Egyptian policy, the PRIME MINISTER stated that the circumstances of the case pre- cluded him from giving anything but a general answer. The Government had an important purpose to accomplish in Egypt, and when that purpose was accomplished they were sincerely desirous to withdraw; but as to a definition of time it was impossible to venture upon anything beyond an expression ofo hope, because the purposes they had in view must regulate the time to be employed. They were in Egypt for the establishment of latv and stability, to secure the fulfilment of international engagements, and to maintain the freedom and security of the Suez Canal. Reasonable progress has been made, and everything had been done thus far which they could possibly have expected, but the Government would not be accelerating the rate of progress were they to undertake to give explanations of a premature character. PRIVATE BILL LEGISLATION.—Mr. SELLAR moved that, in the opinion of the House, the present system of private bill legislation called for the attention of the Government, , and required reform; that in place of private bills which had passed the second reading being referred to select com- mittees, they should be referred for consideration and report to commissions to be established for England, Scotland, and Ireland; and that if any party should appeal against such report, the appeal should be referred to a Parliamentary tribunal composed of members of both Houses of Parliament, in the manner recommended by the joint committee of 1869, with power to award costs.—ln the course of the discussion, Mr. DonsoN announced the agreement of the Government with the first part of the resolution, and at his suggestion Mr. SELLAR adopted the amendment "That this House adheres to•its resolution on private legislation agreed to on the 22nd of March, 1872."—The discussion on this subject I was continued till between eight and nine o'clock, when there was a count out. HOUSE OF LORDS, THURSDAY. The LORD CHANCELLOR introduced a Bill to Amend the Law of Contempt of Court in England and in Ireland A recent case had shown the necessity of amending the law. It would be impossible to abrogate the power of com- mittal for contempt, but the duration of imprisonment ought to be regulated by statute, and not left merely to the discretion of the judge. It was proposed by the Bill to im- prison for three months persons in contempt, the term to be renewed from time to time if the person would not submit. The power should be exercised uniformly by all the Courts, civil, criminal, aid ecclesiastical. The Bill was read a first time.—A Bill introduced her Lord Carlingford for the con- solidation of the law relating to medical practitioners was was also read a first time. The subsequent meeting was held in the lecture-hall, and the Rev. J. M. Fairbourn, the resident minister, presided. The report as to the attendance of teachers and officers was read, and other items connected with the working of the school were brought forward and discussed. appears from a report of a "house dinner" at the Devonshire, Club, London, on Wednesday night, that the Earl of Derby responded to the toast of Her Majesty's Ministers. His Lordship referred to his having recentty entered the Ministry of Mr. Gladstone, and stated that the rest of his political life would be spent in connection with the Liberal party. This passage in his speech was vehe- mently applauded. He further remarked that the Govern- ment were about to give to the greatest city in the world that self-government which the smallest city in the king- dom enjoyed. They also propised to give to tenant farmers what was in equity their own—namely, their nn- exhausted improvements; and, lastly, they desired to repeal. once more a religious test.

SERVICE OF SONG AT THE EARLERTt7WN PRIMITIVE MEznontsr CHAPEL.—On Tuesday evening a service of song. entitled "Little Minnie, or the sunshine of a sister's love," was given in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legh- street, Earlestown, by the united Primitive Methodist choirs of Earlestown and Parr. The proceeds were in aid of the circuit fund. There was only a moderate attendance, but the " service " throughout was of a most enjoyable character. The choir was under the efficient leadership of Mt. W. Banton, and excellently gave the following selec- tions of music:—" That beautiful throne," " Easter hymn," "Are we sowing," "Peace," "Zion', King," and " Will the angels come to me ? " The Misses Smith, of St. Helens, sang effectively the duets "Good bye," and "By and bye," whilst Miss Susan Smith gave "Angels ever bright and fair," and Miss Sarah Smith " Minnie's prayer." A quartette, entitled "Lift the heart," was nicely rendered by the Misses Thompson, Mr. H. Smith, and Mr. R. Spros- ton ; and the Misses Thompson, Mr. Dickens, and Mr. Sproston also gave a piece entitled "Night." Messrs. S. Smith, ef Parr, and William Austin, of Earlestown, presided at the harmonium. At the close of the service the Rev. M. Dickenson, who read the connective reading, asked the con- gregation to mark thdr appreciation of the services of the choir in the usual manner, and the invitation was heartily responded to.

Thereare now 214 farms affected. The new High Sheriff of Lancashire, Mr. Thomas Ashton has appointed Canon Tongue his chaplain. The Menchester Ship Canal .3ill was read a first time in the House of Commies on Monday. CONGEBGATIONIL UNION.—The annual meeting of the Lancashire Congregational Union was held at Southport, on Wednesday, under the presidency of the Rev. T. Willisyo: Manchester. The chairmanzs address was devoted to a con- sideration of the spiritual needs of the churches. In the course of the day a statement .was made with reference to the Congregational Jebilee Fund, which, including £50,0110 from Wales, was said to have reached the sum of MBO,OOC. It had been appropriated to the extinction of debt on chapel buildings, assistance to the Church Aid Society, the support of the colleges, and furtherance in other ways of Congrega- tional interests. At night a public meeting was held in the Chapel-street Church, when Mr. Henry Lee, M.P. presided. The annual 'report was submitted and adopted, and the 1 chairman spoke in hopeful terms of the progress made in re- cent times and the future prospects of the organisation. Other addreeses were delivered by ministers on topics of connexional union. The annual lausiness meeting in con- nection with the Union was held on Thursday, at Southport.; Mr. W. Armitage, the treasurer, presiding.—The treasurer's statement in reference to the ,contributions of the various churches to the funds of the Unien and the sums expended in grants, &c, to aided churches showed a deficiency for the past year of .1:430. The unsatisfactory state of the balance- sheet led to considerable dieeussion, and ultimately it was resolved, on the recommendation of the Committee to re- duce from 12 to 16 per cent the grants to aided churches and stations for the forthcoming year. A resolution was also passed referring to the Executive Committee of the various districte the question of consideving the best means of improving the financial condition of the Union. In the course of the proceedings about £3,100 was voted in grants to the contingent fund, to the Church Aid Society, and other purposes. It was unani- mously resolved to accept an invitation from the congrega- tion at Bury to hold next year's meeting in that town.—On the motion of the Rev. Dr. Ilacia&yen, seconded by Mr. Wheeler, the secretaries and treasurers were re-elected, and .cordially thanked for their past service.s.—The 'ballot for the election of president was taken, and it was announced that ,)3.7.0 voting papers had been handed in. The maority were in favour of the Rev. .L Chater, of Southport, and on the motion of the Rev. T.Cain, seconded 1:0T the Rev. J. Yonge, Mr. Chater was invited to accept the pogtion of president for the coming year. Mr. Chater accepted the invitation.— A .resolution was passel congratulating the Rev. J. Wrecogall, the editer of the Congregational Calendar, upon the production of that work, which, under his care, had become a source of profit to the Union, and requesting him to edit the next nu mber.—The fproceedings closed with a vote of thanks to the chairman. SATURDAY, MARCH 10, 1883.

LATHAM or EGERTON ? That is the all-im- portant question for the electors of Mid-Che- shire. To us it appears the constituency should have very little difficulty in deciding between the two candidates, for they have now been before the electors nearly a fortnight, they have addressed on an average two meetings each daily, and their views on every question specially relating to the agricultural interest as well as on all political questions which affect the agriculturalists only as they affect any other class in the community, are well known. If the enthusiasm manifested at the various meetings be any criterion of the result which may be expected, then, certainly, Mr. LATHAM will be .at the head of the poll, for never before has there been so keen a desire shown to send the Liberal candidate to Parliament. It is generally felt that he has a genuine claim upon the constituency, and no stone will be ie(t unturned to secure his elec- tion. The meetings of his opponent, with one or two exceptions, have been but thinly at- tended, there is a lack of " go " about them, and the candidate himself has proved sadly deficient in all the necessary qualifications to inspire his audiences with. confidence. -4 ,1 ' should take him in, we hope it will only be in the sense that it will discard him ; èe evidently possei,ses but a very limited ac- quaintance with political questions, and he lamentably fails to app, eciate what is wacited in an agricultural district. If, however, one is wanting in intelligence he is not lacking in audacity, the boldness with which he advances some of his peculiar crotchets being rather remarkable, and sometimes amusing. The hon. candidate would get on pretty well if left alone, but it •is when he comes -to be "heckled," as the Scotch say, that ke exposes his ignorance. In his published address he professes a sort of acquiescence in the prin- ciple of compensation being given to tenants for unexhausted improvements, but when in- terrogated about it, as he was the other night at Middlewich, it is found he -is entirely op- posed to giving compensation; freedom of culture and sate of produce, too, are wit'a ;him only conditional; .and on the question c f the extension of the franchise to counties he .-advocates a pro raja qualification which no- 'body understands, and which, for the life of him, he cannot explain himself. These are :the three chief points on which this election will turn, and as on ‘these Mr. EGERTON utters a very uncertain sound it is clear that if he is elected he will not do the Cheshire farmers any good. Mr. I„Anum's promises on these three points are alike ample and clear. With him there is no shuffling.' ' He will, he says, give his best support to a bill to assimi- late the county and borough franchise; he unconditionally advocates full freedom of Gale and culture; and on the:question of compen- sation for unexhausted improvements he would give to the farmer every penny he had ex- pended on the land, and which he had not got back. Can the Mid-Cheshire farmers be so blind to their own interests as to refuse to elect Mr. Latham? If they do, they will in- deed be deserving of censure. Let them not •be hoodwinked by plausible statements to the ',..effect that the Conservatives are their best ,friends. The Conservatives were in office -from 1874 to 1880, they had ample opportun- ities during the six years of giving tangible proof of their friendship to the progress of agriculture, and what, we ask, did it consist of? The passing of a -miserable Agricultural Holdings Bill, the provisions of which were not compulsory, and which were mainly framed in the landlords favour, as all bills passed by a Conservative Government more or less are when landlords are concerned. The present Government have been in office but three sessions, yet they have already been able to give the farmers a foretaste of what they may expect, and they will assuredly receive yet more. As Lord Derby tersely put it on Wed- nesday night, the Liberal Government are going to give to tenant farmers compensation for unexhausted improvements—" what is in equity their own " Hitherto the seats for Mid-Cheshire have been looked upon as be- longing to the Egerton family, and if the members of that family could not fill 'them, then .that whoever was nominated by the family should be elected. Hr ppily there are signs that this feeling is dying, and as this is the last opportunity which an Egerton , will have—for sure it is that when the fran-

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY MARCH 10, 1883.

chise has been extended the territorial in- fluence will no longer be all-potent—of being- 'Line .; screw " is being put on to an- even greater extent than in former contests. I A circular, violating the spirit of the 3allot Act, has been sent round, not only to every tenant on the Egerton estates, but to every voter in the division, asking how each is goino- to vote, and requesting that the document be filled up and returned to the Conservative Central Committee Room. . If the circular is not so filled up then the bailiff is sent round to see what influence he has. Under such circumstances it is nonsense for Mr. Egerton to say that the tenants are as "free as the birds of the air ; " but let us hope this pressure will be of no avail. It only proves the Tories are on the losing side; and another instance of their fear lest the seat should be snatched from them is to be found in the fact that there is being enlisted into Mr. Egerton's service as many paid recruits as possible, the tactics which were followed at Salisbury. On the Liberal side again, the workers are all, or very nearly all, voluntary, they pride themselves on working for principles and a candidate who will practise what he professes, and this, after all, is the feeling which is most likely to command success. The electors must ere this have made up their minds for whom they will vote, and we do not believe they will be so false to themselves and so false to their interests as to reject the candi- dature of their truest friend. We know that of the two candidates Mr. LATHAM is their choice, and why should they be afraid to vote accordingly? Notwithstanding statements to the contrary the ballot is secret there is no possibility of a landlord gettirg to know how his tenants vote ; and r, lying upon that secrecy let the farmer i- of Mid- Cheshire vote for the candidate fter t ieir own heart G. W. LATHAM.

Compulsion was made general in Scotland in 1872, and in that year the average attendance was 213,000, while it is now 4.10,000; and the number of children who passed in reading had risen from 127,000 to 286,000. This shows that education had doubled, while the population had increased by only +oo,ooo out of three millions and a half. It would be idle to suppose that other causes have not been at work, still for these results we are mainly indebted to the opera- tion of the compulsory clauses of the Education Act, and what they have done for England and Scotland they can do for Ireland if only judiciously administered. Great care will, however, have to be exercised in introducing compulsion. What Mr. O'CONNOR POWER calls the "chronic poverty" of the people will be an element of difficulty; but what will be found to be a still more serious hindrance will be the religious element. It will be necessary to act with the most extreme caution so as not to violate the religious susceptibilities of the people, who, as in all other Roman Catholic countries, are, of course, opposed to religion being divorced from education. Still, the Government are nor without hope that in introducing compulsion, which they have promised they will do, a remedy for these difficulties will be found that will be alike practical and effective. We hear very little now of the religious difficulty in England and Scotland, because it is to a great extent a myth; but in the Emerald Isle religious feeling runs much higher. Whenever com- pulsion is introduced into Ireland, however, it will also be necessary to provide more schools and a much better teaching staff if she is to make the progress we anticipate.

A very important and instructive debate on education in Ireland took place in the House of Commons the other evening, and durin), its progress some very interesting facts were elicited. The subject was introduced by Mr. USHAUGHNESSY, the Home Rule member for Limerick city, who moved a resolution declar- ing it to be expedient to introduce into Ire- land the principle of compulsory education, this, however, to be accompanied—as the motion very wisely put it—with such modifi- cations as the social and religious conditions of the country require. Ireland has enjoyed a system of natioriai Pducation for fully half a Century, whilst England and Scotland have been favoured with the inestimable advan- tages of a national Elementary Education Act for iz and to years respectively, yet notwith- standing this fact, the education of the masses in Ireland is very much behind what it is in England and Scotland. It may be urged that the operation of the compulsory clauses in England and. Scotland accounts for the differ- ence in the low degree of education in Ireland as compared with our own country and Scot- land, and though we frankly admit that a very liberal allowance must be made for that, we still think that the causes of illiteracy in the Emerald Isle are to be traced to other sources We are not sure that successive Governments have not much to reproach themselves with for the neglect of Ireland in the matter of education. It may be quite true, as Dr. PLAY- FAIR pointed out the other night, that towards the cost of all possible education in Ireland the State pays no less than 81 per cent., and that the school fees amount to only 18 per cent., leaving only i per cent. to be provided by local aid; but it seems to be equally true that this State aid has been misdirected. Unless good teachers are provided the results are not likely to be satisfactory, and when we reflect that in Ireland there is only one training col- lege to meet the requirements of 7,648 schools, manned by 10600 teachers, it is rather sur- prising, not tnaL bti poogtebb taiab been ntdde in Ireland in the education.. of the rising generation. In this one college 220 students are trained, and on it the State spends £7,755 annually, We are pleasei to learn, however, that in order to meet the deficiency of training colleges the frisk Government have made a recommenda- tion -which has been accepted by the Cabinet, and that the necessary funds to meet the w&rlts of the country in thi9i- regard are to be found by the Treasury. It _ might also at the same .time be desirable to provide more school accommcdation, rhich it is necessary to increase, for whereas In zBBl there were 1,300,000 children within school age in fa-eland, there was accommoda- tion for but 1,155,000, a deficiency that ought to be made up at least before com- pulsion is introduced. In connection with the attendance at school. which is rather on the decrease, :a curious fact was brought out during the debate alluded to, and that was the apparently close connection there exists in Ireland between poverty and education. For instance, th-e average daily attendance of children at Echool in 'SS' was 455.567. show- ing a decrease as compared with 18$o of 14,000; but in the latter year there was an abnormal increase over 1879 of 33,000 an increase which is ascribed to the desire of the children to receive the rations given during, that year, which, as we all know, was a year of exceptional distress. Another fact elicited was this, that the Methodists are the best educated people in Ireland. Of the children of Methodists above five years of age 84i- per cent. can read and write, of the children of Protestant -Episcopalians and Presby- terians 75 per cent. are educated up to this standard, while only 54. per cent of the Roman Catholic children are able to read and write. It is also found, as a matter of fact, that 25 per cent., or a quarter of the population of Ireland, are illiterate at the pre- sent time, not certainly a very encouraging sign after, as we have said, fifty years ex- perience of a national system, yet, in 1841 the per centage of illiterates was 53, so that there• has been a very great advance during the past forty years. In the number of schools there has also been a considerable increase. In 1833 the schools numbered 700 or too. but in 184.0 they had increased to 2,000, in 1860 they were somewhere between 5,000 and 45,000, and now they number 7,648. The diminution in the number of illiterates and the increase in the number of schools clearly indicates, as Mr. TREVELYAN says, that an unlettered generation is passing away. Compulsion will undoubtedly do still more to improve the education of the people as it will to increase the attendance which in Ireland is considerably under an ave:Oage of 8o attendances per child. What compulsion has done for England and Scotland may be gathered from the following figures. In 1870, before compulsion was introduced, the average attendance in England was 1,152,000 ; in 1881, after ii years experience of compulsion, it had risen to 2,860,000. In the same period the number of scholars who passed in reading had risen from 691,000 to 1,776,000— representing an increase in the culture of the

THE DUCHY OF LANCASTER ACCOUNTS —The accounts of the receipts and disbursements of the Duchy of Lancas- ter for the year ended the 31st December, 1852, show that the receipts, including a balance of £19,656, amounted to £87,819. The disbursements were :—Paymentsi made for her Majesty's use to the Keeper of the Privy Purse, £45,000 ; outlay for the benefit of the estate, £2,782; deductions, £2,642; superannuation allowances and charities, £5,428: salary of the Chancellor of the Duchy, £1,659; expenses of management, £6,380: btlances, £23,924 ; total. £7,810. Tan PRUDENTIAL ASSURAIWE COMPANT, LIMITED.—Ia our advertising columns will be found the annual report of this company, which shows that its business is still on the increase. The invested funds, including the paid-up capital, now exceei three millions, viz., ordinary branch £928,176, and industrial branch £2,119,223. The new business of the ordinary branch for the year consists of 7,067 policies, as- suring the sum of £856,148, and producing a new annual premium income of £32,777. The claims of the year amount to £73,621, representing 455 deaths and 24 endowment assurances matured. The annual premium income at the end of the year is £184,949, being an increase of £22,216 over the year 1881. The premiums actually re- ceived during the year in the industrial branch are £2126,0221 3s 11d, as compared with the sum of £1,849,494 18s 5d received during 1881, being an increase of premium receipts of £276,527 556 d. The claims of the year amounted to £773,813, and the total amount of claims paid in this branch is £4,955, 925. The total expenses of this branch as co mpared with those of the previous years show a reduction of nearly 21- per cent on the premium income. The company, it is gratifying to know is now represented in every part of the United Kingdom, and the charges for extension expenses no longer appear in the account. Some conception of the amazing amount of business done by this company may be gathered from the fact that last year there was spent in policy stamps, postage and receipt stamps, no less than £30,760 at the head office only. The Prudential undoubtedly occupies the premier position among the insurance societies; more than one seventh of the entire population of Great Britain and Ireland is insured in it, and its operations are being very rapidly extended and increased.

FOOTBALL: MR. HARDY'S TEAM (SALE) V. RUNCORN.— With a praiseworthy object in view, the Sale club whipped Jai) a team to play a match at Runcorn on behalf of the widow and family of John Garnett, on Wednesday, and a large number of persons witnessed the contest. H. Hughes kicked off for the Runcorn team, and Williams replied, kicking in touch by the half flag, when Alexander entered the home 25, and Howard, from a pass by Thompson, ran in splendidly. The place was, however, notimproved upon. Howard replied to the drop out, and punted well up the field. Johnson moving in another direction, the ball settled down in centre, Hardy making- a good run. Johnson push- ing him in touch by the 25 flag, when Wright kicked to Williams; Mason, checking him, dropped back to Buckley, who entered the home 25, the leather going into touch-in- goal. After this Proctor succer led in gaining the second try, no goal, however, resulting. The home forwards carried the ball with them into Sale's quarters, where Wright appeared like scorin;, Thompson collaring him in I time. Howard's drop out was followed ty a smart run by I Hughes. After the change of ends Hardy started the ball, when, by a combing 1 forward dribble, play ensued on Sale goal-line, and Page gain( I the first try for Runcorn. The point was, however, not improv, 1 upon. Lewis scored the second try from the throw-out, the place-kick again failing. Joule, after playing a good game, gained the third try, which was not improvc 1 upon. Williams soon after gained a free kick. Howard making a capital attempt at goal. In the course of some good play the visitors were crossed, when Atherton, losing possession, Thompson iM7IIC• diately touched down. Up to the finish of the match nothing save minor points was scored, the match ending in favour of Runcorn, viz., 3 tries, 7 minor poiati, to Sale 2 tries, 6 minor points.

CONCERT AT WIDNES.—In aid of the "organ fund" of St. Bede's Chapel, Appleton, a concert was given in the Volunteer Hall, Widnes, on Tuesday evening. There was a crowded audience. A programme of popular music was presented, the performers being Miss Annetta Hallwood (Liverpool), Miss Smith, Mr. Josef Cantor (Liverpool), ledr. Smith, Mr. Joseph Morrison, and Mr. Lawton, and they acquitted themselves in such a manner as to delight the assembled company. WANDERINGS IN ROME.—The inaugural meeting of Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association Historical Society was held on Thursday evening, when in the absence of Mr. W. Handley, the president, Mr. S. C. Beckett occu- pied the chair. There was a fair attendance. The Rev. W. Preston read a paper entitled "Wanderings in Rome," in which were described in a graphic and racy manner the many wondrous and stupendous structures of the "Eternal City." A vote of thanks was accorded him on the motion of Mr. C. Nicksen, seconded by Mr. Pritchard. ASSAULT ON A GIRL AT RUNCoRN.—James McTurk, a man of dissipated appearance, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of having, on Sunday, the 18th February, unlawfully assaulted Sarah Booth, a girl of seven years of age. From the evidence of , Charlotte Ainsworth, it seemed that on the day named the I prisoner was in a state ot intoxication in Percival's-lane, where he stayed talking to a number of children. He after- ' wards took the prosecutrix, a bright-looking child, into a I passage. Mrs. Ainsworth, hearing a scream, went there I and saw the prisoner in the act of assaulting the girl. The prisoner then behaved in a very violent manner to Mrs." Ainsworth and the mother of the girl.—He was committed to gaol for a month without the option of a fine. WIDNES I OCAL BOARD.—On Wednesday a special meet- ing of the Widnes Local Board was held to consider the expediency of oppesing or otherwise, the London and North-Western Railway Extension Bill, and the Bill for the construction of the Ship Canal to Manchester. Mr F. A. Goss:age, presided, and there were present :—Dr. O'Keede, Messrs. Carey, Handly, Pankhurst, Shuttleworth, Sadler, Webster, Johnson, Manley, Midwood, Wright, and Allen (clerk).—lt was decided, on the motiou of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Carey, that the Board should oppose both bills' and that Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., solicitors, and Mr. Allen, the clerk, be empowered to take the requisite steps. Messrs. Gossage, Carey, Handley, Wright, and Sad- ler, were appointed a committee to watch the progress of the hills. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, RUNCORN. The Rev. J. Billington, on Sunday preached ewo sermons in this place of worship in aid of the Home and Foreign Missions. There were good congregations. On Wednesday evening the annual Missionary Society meeting was held, the Rey. J. Billington in the chair. Mr. E. Gandy read the report, which showed that the society had made progress during the past year. The Rev. T. Sherwood, of Liverpool, and the Rev. H. T. Chapman, of Littleborough, delivered in- structive addresses in which they made stirring appeals for missionary assistance, both on the ground of the wants of the heathen, and for the advancement of our own spiritual life, and the performance of duty imposed by love to the Christ that died for the salvation of the whole human race. The gross estimate of the cost of the naval service for the ensuing year is set down at £11,582,758, against £11,155,909 for 1882-83, giving an increase upon the gross of £426,849. The pro- gramme of shipbuilding works in the home yards and at Malta estimates for the employment of 1,375 more men at borrO and 397 more at Malta than were shown in the pre- vious year's estimates. Daring the year it is proposed that the Royal dockyards shall be occupied on 36 vessels of all classes, including twelve ironclads, three corvettes, four sloops, five steel steam cruisers, eleveu composite gun vessels and boats, and one paddle-wheel vessel. 15,172 tons are to be built during the year, of which 11.224 are to be armoured and 3,948 unarmoured. In addition to these private ship- builders are to turn out 1,982 tons of armoured construction and 2,270 tons of unarmoured. including 27 torpedo boats. This gives an aggregate of 19 644 togs to be built in the year, as against 20,142 in 1882 83.

ALLEGED TIIEFT FllO3l THE PERSON AT RIINCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. A. Thomas and Colonel Talbot, a middle-aged man, named Benjamin Rooney, was brought up in custody charged with stealing a pursecontaining 9s 94, the property of Ellen Peers.-From the statement of Mr. Superintendent Williamson it ap- ptared that Mrs. Peers, who lives on Mill Brow, on Satur- day morning was on her way to the market, when she stopped at a stall where a miscellaneous lot of goods were offered for sale. She purchased an article, but on putting her band in her pocket she discovered that her purse had been abstracted. She accused a woman who was standing near, with the robbery, but she denied the charge, and ex- pressed her willingness to accompany the prosecutrix "any- where." The woman then went across the street, and was seen to give the prisoner something. The prisoner hurried away, but he was watched, and seen to enter the closet on the premises of a photographer, where the missing purse was subsequently found. The woman escaped, but the prisoner was afterwards apprehended by P.C. Noden. He was searched, and about I.oi was found upon him.—The case was adjourned until Thursday. when the prisoner was again brought up before Mr. W. Bankes, and in com- pany with Margaret Rooney, his wife, was committed for trial at the next Knu'sford assizes. Mr. O. Leak defended.

It is estimated that with the expemles, Mr. Biggar's love adventure will cost him altogether about £l,OOO. The schooner Pacific of Dublin, with coals, lying in the dock at Newry, was destroyed by fire on Thursday night, and the mate, who was asleep, was burnt to death. The sentence of death passed upon the peactrer, James Smith, for shooting one of Lord Stair's aatnekeepers in Ayr- shire has been commuted to penal servitude for life. Lord Sherborne died, on Tkursd?y, at his seat, Sherborne Lodge, near Northleach, Gloucestershire in his 79th year. He was a Conservative, and is succeeded by his son, Hon. Edward Lennox Dutton. An engine driver, named Pankhurst, while engaged, on Thursday night, at Tunbridge Wells station in lighting a fire under a water crane, was knocked down by the Dover mail; and he died in a few minutes. Richard Tasker, 31 years of age, collier, committed sui- cide by cutting his throat with a razor, at Baxenden, on Thursday. Deceased was called unon by another collier to go to his work, when he was found lying in the back kitchen of his house, quite dead, with a large gash. in his throat.. Doing the high gale on Thursday a singular fatality hap- pened to a young man named Thomas Powell, of Groy- saney, Mold. 'The deceased was entering the timber yard of a joiner for the purpose of leaving his cart, when the gale blew one of the folding doers against the cart with such violence that it upset, and falling on deceased's chest in- dicted such dreadful injuries that he died almost imme- diately. Yesterday the minders employed at the Alexandra New and Old Mills, and Acre Mill, Oldham, struck work. The operatives want an additional half-penny per thousand hanks on counts ranging from thirteen and a half to twenties, and above twenties a halfpenny per thousand on spinning for twining. In the New Mills, the employer offers an extra halfpenny for all ; in the Old Mill, where men from a penny to twopence accordin g to quality, the enl- ployer offers an advance from a halfpenny to a penny.

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held at the Board..room, Bridgewater-street, on Wednesday. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were also present Messrs. J. Simpson, T. Norman, James Pritchard, Peter Briscoe, and F. Eigby (clerk.)—The Visitor's report stated the returns from the public elementary schools for February, 1883, were as follows: Certified Government accommodation, 2,716; total number on the rolls, 2,933; number on the rolls corresponding period of last year, 2,841; increase in the number on the rolls, 62; total average attendance, 2,129.2; average attendance corresponding period of last year, 2,041.5; increase is average attendance, 87.7 ; average attendance for the year 1874, 125 2; increase in average attendance as eimpared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, 8772; acconl- m-)dation in excess of average attendance, 586 8; number on the rolls in excess of accommodation, 187 ; number in atten- dance at private adventure schools under 9d per week, 73. In the returns for the past month ending February 23rd, I have to report an improvement in the attendance of boys and girls as compared with the preceding month, but there. is still a decrease in the attendance of infants. Whooping cough is prevalent, and many infants are still suffering from severe colds and sore throats. During the past month 90 notices have been served.—Mr. Bowyer was ordered to pro- secute in 18 cases.

TRICKS OF RAILWAY TRAVELLING: EXTENSIVE FRAUDS. —At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Monday, George Peach, a middle-aged man, was charged with attempting to defraud the London and North-Western Railway Company. On Saturday night the prisoner booked third class from Liver- pool, Lime-street, to Edge Hill, and having passed, the barrier, entered the 10-50 train for Widnes. He was watched by Detective-sergeant Stamford and another official who also entered the train. When the train arrived at Edge Hill the prisoner did not alight. He continued in the train until it stopped at Widnes, where be alighted, and walking up to a porter, asked him if be had seen a woman and two children, for whom he was searching, anywhere about. The porter replied in the negative. De- tective-sergeant Stamford then went to him and asked him for his ticket. He replied that he had not come by train, but bad been on the station since one o'clock that day. Eventually, however, he produced the Edge Hill ticket, and was taken into custody. The railway gompany wished to press the case, as they had reason to believe that frauds similar to the one practised had been perpetrated on a very extensive scale. Recently a large number of Edge Hill tickets had been unaccounted for. In the month of January no fewer than 1,202 were missing, and in corrsequence of this all the trains on Saturday last were watched for the purpose of catching the culprits. In the case of the prisoner the offence was aggravated by the fact that he had former :y been in the service of the railway company, and could not thus ; plead ignorance as an excucc.—The prisoner, in default of plying a rine of 2)s and costs, was sent to gaol for 14 lays

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
SINKING OF AN EMIGRANT SHIP. SIXTY-FIVE LTV E,g Ins

The smack Sir Stafford Northcote arrived at Hull yester. day, having on board five persons rescued from the Leith steamer Navarre, which foundered last Tuesday, on Little Fish Bank. The Navarre was bound from Copenhagen for Leith, via Christiansand, which place she left on Sunday night, having on board 50 emigrants. besides other Passen- gers!, the total on board being 81. The vessel was disabled, and hove on her beam ends in the gale on Monday night, and when fallen in with by the smack appeared to be sinking. The fishermen launch(' a boat, but it broke away and was lost. Lines were got ready, but before they could be used the Navarre ; turned over and sank. Just before she went down seven Scotch and three Norwegian sailors went away with the only remaining boat, and were seen to get on board a Dutch cod smack lying near. The Sir Staff ,rd l`Tinthcote saved one young lady and four men, and the Hull smack Florence Louise picked up another man. All the rest went down with the vessel, the total loss being sixty-five souls. The Sir Stafford Northcote also brought in the body of a child whose father had been saved, and an inquest will be held upon it. The Navarre was an iron vassel, and was built at Liverpool in 1866, being owned by Mr. James Currie, 16, Bernard-street, Leith. Her gross tonnage was 855.

div.head: MID-CHESHIRE ELECTION.
div.p: THE MID-CHESHIRE ELECTION.

The writ for the election of a member for Mid-Cheshire in the room of the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, who, con- sequent upon the death of his father, has been raised to the peerage, was receired yesterday (Friday) week, and en Saturday the Sheriff and the Returning Officer notified that all nominations must be delivered between the hours of eleven and one o'clock on Thursday the Bth inst., in the grand jury-mom of the Court-house at Knutsford. The polling is tixed for Weanesday next. Both parties are, and have been, actively at work since the seat be- came vacant, and both are sanguine of success. The Liberals, who feel they have nothing to loose and much to gain, are working with an enthusiasm never before known; whilst the Conservativee, knowing that they have a weak candidate, are not leaving a stone unturned to retain the , seat in the Egerton family. The prominent features in j favour of the Liberal caudidate are that in the previous ' contests he has brought out the fact that the Liberal prin- ciples have gradually advanced in Mid-Cheshire, that he would be a real redresser of farmers' grievances, and that his opponent, though bearing the Conservative and terri- torial name of Ege ton, is hardly known at all in the county, and cannot, therefore, count on the suppert which was al- ways accorded to the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton (now Lord Egerton), who was to a great extent popular with the farming class, amongst whom he freely mixed in public and private. So far as the farming class is con- cerned, it is but fair to say—and the Liberals at their meet- ings do not deny it—that the Egertons are acknowledged to be good landlords. That no doubt will satisfy some, and a few may not care to look for any other qualification in the candidate they support. The great majority of farmers, however, desire something more than this, and will have definite promises from the man they support on legislation for which they have been hoping for many long years. Mr. Latham more than meets the wishes of this numerous class of farmers, and be will undoubtedly receive their undivided support. Long before legislative compensation for unex- bausted improvements came within range of Government promise, Mr. Latham was a strong advocate for it, and at many an agricultural meeting he enforced the views which he enunciates in the -present campaign and which will be acceptable to the tenant farmer It is a significant fact, on this portion of Mr. Latham's pro- gramme, that so great an authority on agriculture and what is needed to improve the farmers' condition as Mr. Thomas Rigby, secretary oi the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture, should have come forward publicly to support the Liberal candidate. If the proposals of Mr. Latham are espoused by such a cautious man as Mr. Thomas Rigby they may be taken to be sound, and to meet all that teuant farmers desire at the hands of the present Government. At any rate, Mr. Rigby's recognition of the Liberal candidate's claims on the farming classes will have great weight in the contest. With reference to the agricultural interest, the Hon. Alan de Egerton cannot by any means know near so much about its requirements in this part of Cheshire as his brother, the late Conservative representative, and his views will not be accepted as of much political value. What he suggests is that the tenant should by agreement with his landlord secure compensation for unexhausted improvements, and ho would afford relief to the distressed agricultural interest by assisting the local rates with contributions from chases of property now exempted. Upon the whole the views of the majority of farmers will coincide with those of Mr. Latham. The only danger to the Liberal cause is the old one of too much confidence, and the belief, to Use a sporting phrase, that there is "nothing to beat ; " but it should not be forgotten that the Tories, a weak candidate notwithstanding, are working as though the return of the Opposition to power depended upon their providing the Hon. Alan Egerton with a seat in the House of Commons. General politics, of course, enter into this contest, but they are more discussed in the towns of the division than in the rural districts. It is in the towns where the Liberal strength lies, and Mr. Latham may anticipate good majorities in Congleton, Altrincham, Run- corn, Northwich, Sale, and probabiy Sandbach. Middle- wich, Tatton, and Knatsford (which is at the very doors of the residence of the Egertons) whine doubt be largely Tory We append a copy of a circular which has been issued by the Tories :

MID-CHESHIRE FLE^TION, 1883. Central Committee- roomy, Knutsford, Fa). 27th, beg to enclose a copy of the addrees of the Hon. Alan act Tatton itgerton, the Conservative candidate at the approaching -Tection for this division, and to solcit on his berialf your vote anu May I ask the favour of y orre-iirnit.g the annexed paper by newt", . ortwt nct whether tw. opt. Shft -311- i 11.; `617", /IV. cga.ggg clan vant, LANC ,L BENTLEY, the Hon. Alan de Patton Egerton's Central Agent.

On the opposite page blanks are left for the elector to say whether it is his intention to vote for the Hon. Alan de 'Batton Egerton or not, and whether he will require a railway order for his journey At the meeting of Mr. Latham's friends, at Knutsford, on Saturday, the Liberal candidate very properly laid much stress on this circular. It has not been confined, as might be expected, to the tenants supposed to be staunch supporters of whatever candidate the House of Egerton puts forward, but has been sent broadcast throughout the division. Mr. Latham very properly characterised this as a corrupt prac- tice, if it did not border on infringement of the Ballot Act. The fact that the circular has been sent to ev ry elector will not relieve the Tories from the suspicion that it is intended for the tenant farmers under Tatton Hall influence. It is strange that, though the circular arrived at every elector's house on the very morning succeeding Lout Egerton's funeral, the morality of issuing it was not discussed until several days afterwards. One would have though that the Liberals vrottld have replied very generally with an intimation to the electors that they need not pay the slightest attention to the polite invitation of the Tcries, hut we have seen no caution, except the one pronounced by Mr. Latham at Knutsford, who assured the farmers that the:, would, under the ballot, record their votes without the slightest fear of anyone knowing how they vote. The circul ir will undoubtedly have a prejudicial effect an Mr. Latham's candidature in certain districts, for it has been intimated by the Torie, at former elections that it would be found out who voted against the Tory candi- date, and a good few farmers are obliged to vote one way, when if left to their free and unfettered choice they would vote another.

The division of Mid-Cheshire, which has a population: of 120.289, contains 9 915 electors on the present register, from which will have to be deducted deaths and removals. At the recent revision the Liberals claimed a net gain of 227 and the Conservatives a net gain of 220. The election of 1880 was fought on a register containing an aggregate roll of 8,863, but it was reduced by duplicates and deaths to an actual number of 8.267. On that occasion Mr. Latbatn was 493 below the lion. Wilbraham Egerton and 326 below Mr. P. E. Warburton. The Liberal gain on the revision being 227, it will be seen that the prospects of Mr. Latham • are very bright ; and as between 1873, when he first con- tested the division, and 1880, when he reduced his min- ority from 1,390 to 326, it may safely be inferred that he must have mace a corresp nding reduction between the last election and the present time. There are many signs that territorial influence is not so potent as it used to be, and in addition to this advantage Mr. Latham goes into the fight with the united support of the Liberal party. The total elec- tors we have named above are distributed into the following fourteen polling districts :

On the day great distance some b:xvee arrangements places are from Knntsford will entail extensive to secure the due delivery of the ballot- election. but the re- turning-officer anticipates that the result wille'be lEnnwn by about nine o'clock on the evening of the day of - - -

- - A circular has ben issued by the Manchester, Salford, and District Beer and Wine Trade Association calling upon the beer and wine retailers of Mid-Cheshire to support the can- didature of the Hon. Alan de Tatten Egerton. It will be interesting to many active politicians to know that the Liberals are carrying on their operations by maps of voluntary helpers, while the Conservatives are employing paid canvassers. But notwithstanding the pecuniaryin- ducement which the Guservatives hold out to their agents it is generally admitted that their organisation is not superior, if indeed it is as good, as that of the Liberals. If the enthusiasm of the Liberal workers is sufficient to induce them to continue unremitting and energetic exertions on be- half of Mr. Latham until the close of the poll, then they will, , there is every reason to believe, have beta largtly instru.
mental in electing as Liberal member for Mid-Cheshire a man who has fully earned the title of farmer's friend.

div.head: MEETINGS OF MR. LATHAM'S SUPPORTERS. NORtHWIC H.
div.p: MEETINGS OF MR. LATHAM'S SUPPORTERS. NORtHWIC H.

Mr. Latham addressed a large meeting of his supporters at the Drill Hall, Northwich, last (Friday) evening week. The feeling in this town, which is the centre of the Che- shire salt trade, runs rather strongly in Mr. Latham's favour, and the gathering of the evening was enthusiastic. The chair was taken by Mr. TuomAs RIGBY, of Sutton, a well-known Cheshire agriculturist. He spoke of the reluctant manner in which justice was dealt to the tenant farmers by those who had the power. Tenant farmers must assert their independence. He. pointed out that Mr. Latham's proposals in this regard were much more liberal than those of Mr. Alan Egerton, the Conservative candidate. Mr. G. W. LATHAM was well received. He said he had made some converts to tenant-right, including, he believed, his opponent. This tardy convert had come forward, and said he would not object to compensation being given to the tenant for his improvements if the landlord bad not already contracted with him on that 9ubject. Surely Mr. Egerton would not say he would not punish a man for steal- ing,.provided that the man whose property was stolen agreed that the property should be stolen. (Laughter and cheers.) It was dishonest of the landlord to take the pro- perty which the tenaat farmer had in the land without com- pensation, and such compensation ought to be compulsory. (Cheers.) After pointing out that Mr. Egerton did not promise to support the extension of the franchise, Mr. Latham went on to speak of the salt duties, and claimed for Lord Ripon, as a Liberal, credit for having put those duties on a satisfactory footing. A resolution in support of Mr. Latham was unanimously carried.

div.head: KNUTSFORD.
div.p: KNUTSFORD.

Mr. Latham addressed a meeting at Knntsford, on Satur- day. He was accompanied on the platform by Mr. Corn- wallis West, and Mr. Summers, M.P. for Staleybridge. Mr. E. L. Ashworth, of Manchester, presided. . . . .

Mr. LATHAM commented on the issue of the circular to the Tatton tenants. He said that that, if not a corrupt practice, was plainly, to his mind, an offence against the Ballot Act. By that Act it was intended that voters should be enabled to record their vote in secret, and the object of the circular was that the agent might follow and write down "yes "or "no " at each farmhouse. He hoped that the farmers would on the polling day record their votes without fear or favour for the man whom they believed would do his best to redress existing grievances and advance England on the paths of Liberal progress. As to the equalisation of the franchise and the compensation to tenant farmers, he pointed out that Mr. Egerton had only given an uncertain sound, and had actually spoken at Sandbach of giving every man a vote pro rata, a phrase Mr. Latham expressed his inability to understand. _
