div.head: HILTON.
div.p: HILTON.

Mr. Latham commenced his campaign in the Runcorn district on Tuesday. He arrived in the town by train about 12 o'clock, when he was driven to the residence of Mr. R. Shaw, President of the Runcorn Liberal Association. At two o'clock Mr. Latham, accompanied by Mr. Shaw, drove to Halton, where lee addressed a meeting in the old Court- room ol the Castle. A cold, biting wind swept the summit Of the hill, and doubtless, prevented many farmers and others, who would have to drive a long distance from put- ing in an appearance. There was,nevertheless,a fair audience, and the proceedings were presided over by Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P., of Frodsham. There were also present : Messrs. R. Shaw, William Handley, and Joseph Stokes.— The CHAIRMAN briefly introduced Mr. LATrrAm, who explained his views on the land ques- tion and other matters appertaining to farming. Alluding to the rates, he said they were very high, and had not been reduced during the last few years. Yet, during those years, they had had considerable subsides from Govern- ment. How was it then that the rates had not diminished? It was simply because these subsidies from the Crown led to increased extravagance, and what be should like to see was the rates divided between landlord and tenant.
In answer to a question as to what were his views on the county franchise,...
Mr. LATHAM Said every ratepayer had a big stAke in the country, and ought, therefore, to have a voice in the ad- ministration of its affairs. (Cheers.)
WESTON.

Mr. Latham was then driven across the country N the Prospect Inn, in the large room of which hostelry there was a large and enthusiastic gathering of workmen and others. Mr. James Handley presided, and there were also present, in addition to the candidate, Mr. Robert Shaw, the Rev. J. D. Thomas (of Runcorn), T. Handley, George Moss, T. Stringfellow, itc. The CHAIRMAN, who was received wtth load applause, said he had the greatest satisfaction in bringing begore them not a member of the Metropolitan Board of Works but one who for many years had taken the deepest interest in every movement having for its object the well-being of the in- habitants of Cheshire. But if there was one qualification more than another possessed by their candidate if was his fitness to represent in the House of Commons, the true in- terest of the farmers—in fact he had so distinguished him- self in that respect as to have earned for himse county the title of the farmers' friend. (Cheers. There was, however, yet another reason why it was desirable that Mr. Latham should be chosen as their representative, and that was perhaps the most important of all. He had de- clared himself to be a supporter of that Government which they, along with him, believed to be the best Government that had ever ruled over this kingdom. (Cheers.) In sup- porting and electing Mr. Latham they would have in the House of Commons not only a renresentative of the "rights of property," but a faithful pleader for the "rights of the people." (Cheers.) Mr. Le-raam, who was heartily received, said since com- ing into the neighbourhood he had handed him a newspaper Which contained an account of the Conservative meeting held in Weston, which bristled with so many misstatements that he really could not begin what he wanted to say without in some measure answering them. The first state- ment made by Canon Barclay was a comparison between him (Mr. Latham) and Lord Egerton as to their beneficence to Church education. He did not pretend to be able to com- pare himself with Lord Egerton in the munificence of his gifts—be had not the income. He bad not built churches and schools, but he had according to his means given land for churches and for schools, and for chapel. (Hear, hear,

div.head: EXAMINER SATU'RDAY, MARCH 10, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATU'RDAY, MARCH 10, 1888.

and cheers.) Then Canon Barclay said that whilst Lord' Egerton had supported Church schools, he (Mr. Latham) had done everything he could to destroy the Weaver schools. Now, except so far as credit was due to a man who found out a plan, he could take no credit to himself for doing that. Mater, a the matter was this : That the Weaver Church Act was passed some 40 years ago. There was a clause put into that Act which empowered the trustees to erect a school that would cost not more than £l5O, to be attached to each church; and that the ministers of the said churches should teach in the said schools under the direction of a bishop. There was not one single word said about schoolmasters for these schools, nor about the trustees paying salaries to the master. All that was meant was that there should be a Sunday school—Xlso would not do for a day school—in which the minister of each of the three Weaver schools should teach. It happened that 30 years ago that the trustees had been giving grants to schools not belonging to the Weaver: Churches, and they took an opinion of the two great counsel of the day—Sir Frederick Thesieger and Mr. Cawling—as to whether it was legal to do so. The counsel said it was illegal, and at the end of the opinion the former informed the trustees—" Indeed I am bound to inform the trustees that they have no right to ;pay anything to the schools which are con- nected with the churches." Well, the history of the thing was that the trustees gave the management of their schools to five clergymen who were also trustees, and somehow or other without the trustees knowing anything about it, these payments for school education connected with the Church of England were made out of the money belonging to the ratepayers of Cheshire to the extent of about £5OO a year. (Cheers.) A quarrel arose between the clergyman at YC'eston Point and Canon Barclay, who was appointed one of the managers of the schools. That clergy- man said he would not have Canon Barclay going into his school at all. He (Mr. Latham) thought it was a most extraordinary thing that the trustees, who alluded to the differences at their meeting, should pay £5OO a year to schools, over which the Bishop had the management and who spent the money; so he read the Act carefully, and at once saw that they had no power to spend the money. The matter was brought forward at the next meeting of the trustees and every trustee—Conservative and Liberal— agreed that they had not the slightest power to spend that money, and that its payment should be discontinued. It was so clear that the trustees had been doing what was illegal that the matter never came to the vote. Mr. Christopher Bushell proposed that the pay- ments should go on for six months, but he (Mr. Latham)iproposed an amendment that they should be continued until the end of the school year, whether it be nine months, or six months, er three months, but he afterwards withdrew his proposal, and let Mr. Bushell have way. That was the whole account. (Cheers.) If in con. sequence they had to have a School Board at Weston,ltie rate would not be heavy, as the Weaver and the Chemical' Works were rated at their full valuation. He now came to what gave him a great deal more pain than that, which was simply an attack upon his judgment as to whether Church schools were right or wrong. Another clergyman, from whom one would expect Christian charity—(hear, hear, and cheers)—made a most violent attack upon him. He did not dare to say anything himself, but he said if rumour were true, he believed the principles of Mr. Latham were notvery far removed from those of Mr. Bradlaugh. (" Shame.") He (Mr. Latham) would not answer on the hustings any ques- tion at all as to what his religious opinions were. He con- sidered that was not a matter that anybody had a right to require from a candidate. (Hear, hear.) But a statement of the kind he had referred to was meant to throw dirt, and he thought it was as well to put up his umbrella to keep it off. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) He :challenged Mr. Preston and he asked him to contradict the rumour that he had been kind enough to spread wherever he had gone, and say that he (Mr. Latham) had not the slightest symplthy with the principles of Mr. Bradlaugh—that he hated and despised them. (Cheers.) Mr. Latham then criticised the state- ments of Mr. Glover, and spoke of tenant right, fixity of tenure, extension of the county franchise, etc.; and he was frequently cheered. He satisfactorily answered several questions asked by Mr. S. Yarwood with regard to the franchise. Another ratepayer asked' if he could tell what Mr. Egerton meant by pro rota franchise? Mr. LATHAM : I wish I could. (Loud laughter.) He supposed Mr. Egerton meant that a man who paid £5 a year should have one vote, a man who paid £lO two votes, and a man who had £40,000 a year like his brother 400 votes. (Laughter. A voice: That's Tory democracy. (Re- newed laughter,) Mr. T. HANDLEY moved "That this meeting is of opinion that Mr. G. W. Latham is a fit and proper person to repre- sent this envision of Cheshire in Parliament." He spoke in eulogistic terms of Mr. Latham's abilities, and contrasted the sound financial position of the present Government with the blundering of their predecessors. Referring to the Rev. William Preston's remarks, he observed that Mr. Latham was a member of the Church of England, and be bad shown his Christianity by giving land on which to build churches, and also to build a chapel. (A Voice: "That was the mistake.") He had also given proof of his practical Christianity and godliness by instituting a reformatory for the reclamation of children— (hear, hear, and cheers)-27 years ago. Such rumours as Mr. Preston made the subject of a speech should be beneath the notice of everyone. A few years ago Mr: Preston built a house for himself, and he was quite willing to take the subscriptions of Nonconformists, but he had taken advantage of every opportunity to denounce Dissenters. (Cheers.) Mr. ROBERT Slim seconded the resolution, and, alluding to the meeting on the previous evening, said Canon Barclay appeared to think that the reason why they should send another Tory to Parliament was because the late Lord Egerton of Tatton had given £5OO to build a church. He taunted the Conservatives with having no policy to place before the eleotors, and refuted various statements made the previous evening. There was one thing that pained him in that election, and that was t 6-6 a__.minister of the Gospel, who ought to have but in the Bible, which he 'had stuchea; "Speak evil of no man "—could listen to rumours of such a nature, and repeat them as if. they were true. He was sorry for the Conservatives if a minister of the Gospel had nothing better to talk to the electors of Mid-Cheshire about than some simple wicked rumour. (Cheers.) The Rev. J. D. THOMAS supported the resolution, after which it was carried by acclamation. Mr. LATHAM replied, and proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was seconded by Mr. &Law, and carried.

who stated Mr. Latham was an infidel uttered a calumny. (Cheers.) What did the scriptures say, "Wherefore by their fruits shall ye know them "—(cheer)—and the good fruits of his honoured friend Mr. Latham, which he had poured for many years into the drain of the people of that district were an abundant answer to the CaluinnieS which ..snarr% paid parsons had uttered against him.. kiJoi:iu

_ Mr. G. W. LATHAM, who was received with a great out- burst of cheering, over and over again repeated, then stepped forward to address the meeting. He said he remembered with gratitude that the electors of Runcorn had done their best for hint in former times, and he believed, spite of the lies of parsons and the sneers of their opponents, that they would do their best for him once again. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) He believed they were going to win this time, for their opponents save in an excessively bad temper, as if they were going to lose. (Laughter.) He would pass by a good deal of the bad language that the Conservative candi- date had used at Winsford, and a strange utterance of a good friend of his at Mobberley, but he would like to ask those present to listen to a few words of the opening address of the chairman (Mr. Harter) at the Mobberley meeting. (Hear, hear.) The chairman had said that the feeling of regret which they felt at Loid Egerton's death was mingled with surprise and indignation that the return of the Hon. Mr. Egerton to Parliament should be opposed at all—(loud laughter) ; that Mr. Egerton was a gentleman born in their midst, and a member of a family whose claim to the respect and esteem of the electors- had been well proved— (renewed laughter)—and the chairman of the Mobberley meeting asked who Mr. .Latham was; who had come forward to stand between them. (Laughter and hear, hear.) He would tell them who Mr. Latham was. (Loud cheers.) Mr. Latham was the chosen candidate of the Liberal Two Hundred" of Mid-Cheshire. (Cheers.) He was no nominee of an aristocratic house—(hear, hear)—whose candidature had been forced upon them by the hangers-on of the great and those who picked up the crumbs which fell from the great men's tables. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Latham was not one of the privileged classes, who simply had lived upon what they could get from the poor, but be was a man sprung from the people, and of the people, and desiritrg to do what he could for the people. (Loud and prolonged cheering.) He stood not on the memories of the past, but upon his promises for the future, (Hear, hear.) He depended not upon his ancestors, but upon himself. (Hear, near.) tie did not crave to be a "natural" representative, but he claimed to be a representative who, after due consideration, they had chosen. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) That was what Mr. Latham had been—(laughter and cheers)—what he at pre- sent was—(loud cheers)—and what he hoped to be hereafter. (Renewed cheering.) He was now their candidate, but he believed that before many days were passed, in spite of all opposition' and the slander, sneering, and all the talk they lately heard, be would be their accepted member, repre- enting them in Parliament. (Hear, hear.) Coming to the ieir hugeness of the meeting, and comparing his views of the great slibjects of the day with his opponent's, he found that the first difference between them was that he (Mr. Latham) was in favour of the assimilation of the county franchise— (hear, hear, and cheers)—while Mr. Egerton utterly ignored the fact that such a question was before the public. (Laugh- ter.) Mr. Egerton had said that he would give the county franchisepro rata—(a laugh)—and he (Mr. Latham) had not quite clearly been able to make out or understand what a pro rata franchise meant. (Loud laughter.) He could only think it was something like the way they had at vestries, and Poor - law Boards, where if a man paid £5 rent he got one vote, and if he paid £lO he got two. (Hear, hear.) In that case they might expect Mr. Egerton's brother, with his £40,000 or so, to have 400 votes. That was what he called the pro rata representa- tion, but he did not think it would suit the men of Runcorn. I (" No, no," and cheers.) He, for one, could not see why a man, because he was rich, should have more voting powers ' than a poor man. (Hear, hear.) The poorest man in the room, if he had a wife and children, was as much concerned in the good government of the country as the richest man in England. (Hear, hear.) Depend upon it, they would never get their full rights in the counties before they had the franchise given them. With regard to the land ques- tion, he believed that it perhaps concerned the agricultural labourers more than any other men, and it was time that they should have men to look after their interests. (Cheers.) It was the duty of every Englishman, whatever party he belonged to, to support the present Govern- ment of Ireland—(cheers)—and these servants of ours, the Lord-Lieutenant and Chief Secretary, who held their lives in their hands—(hear, hear)—and who, for the sake of their country, were content to go through all those dangers, day by day and night by night. And no man had any right, in the smallest de- gree, to lessen their authority. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to him, that if there was one reason at the present moment why the Conservative party should not be strengthened, it was because it had shown itself so perfectly callous to any at- tempt to support her Majesty's Government, and because they had in every way discredited the authority of the Irish Government. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) There was another peint. The improvement in trade since the present Govern- ment came into power had been. questioned, and, in reply, he was in a position to say that it had, within the last three years, slowly, it might be, but surely changed for the better. (Cheers.) For instance, the Clearing House returns for 1879 were £4,959,000,000; in 1880, the first year of the Liberal Government, they were £5,710,000,000; in 1881, £6,535,000,000; and in 1882, £6,20,000,00C.,The exports dur- ing the last four years had been £131,000,000 first; second £146,000,000; third, £155,000,000; and fourth,Lls7,ooo,ooo. But it must be remembered that their best market was their home market, and as long as agriculture was in its present depressed condition, they could not but expect that the trade, which lived upon agriculture, should be depressed also. They might hope and trust that the sun would shine and dry weather continue; and perhaps by and by they would find that America would consume more of its own goods, and not send them to compete with British products. The land question, which occupied the public mind largely, was not simply a question as between landlord and tenant; it was a question that concerned workingmen in every possible way, because he believed it might be found possi- tAfri ' n`h "besrAiF'and by by peasant a vela .be torehip. (Cheers.) If th.y laws of settlement, manage so to discourage the accumula- tion of great estates so that land might come into the market in smaller quantities, and men be tempted to buy small lots of land, build houses on them, and cultivate the ground, he thought they would be introducing a safeguard and a bulwark to the constitution which ought not lightly to be despised. (Hear,'hear.) Besides these reforms of the land laws, and others that he had mentioned in his address, there were great alterations needed in the laws of settlement. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, he asked the electors to send him to Parliament, that he might have an opportunity of advocating the above, amongst so many other reforms, which it appeared to him would be a real benefit to the country, would strengthen its constitution, and would clear away the troublesome difficulties which occasionally arose up in their path. (Loud and continued cheers.) Mr. WOODALL, M.P., said, they had in office a Govern- ment which was admitted by friends and foos alike to be one of the strongest that had been known in modern history. (Cheers.) Its front bench was- full of capable men, who were only overshadowed by the gigantic figure which towered above them—(cheers)—but, without its chief, he ventured to aay that the Liberal Government of to-day was stronger in an administrative capacity than any Government which the opposite side of the House could possibly produce. (Hear, hear.) He appealed to them to send to the Commons a man who would support this Government. In Mr. Latham they had one who had inspired confidence in the agricul- tural classes throughout England, and who was eminently qualified to help forward a just measure of land reform.

Mr. JOHN SIMPSON said when last Mr. Latham came for- ward as the candidate for Mid-Cheshire, the people were groaning under a Conservative Government, the remem- brance of whose dreadful doings was almost enough to make one shudder. (Laughter and cheers.) They had now at the head of the best Liberal Government which this country had ever seen, the first statesman in Europe—(loud cheers) —who, as a man and a statesman, had secured for himself a place in the estimation of his own countrymen, such as no member of a Government had ever occupied before. (Re- newed cheering.) lie had no confidence in the party to which Mr. A. Egerton belonged. (Hear, hear.) During the last 51 years the present Lord Egerton and his father had done so little for the reform of any real abuses, that he thought it was quite time that they should have a change in the representation of the County of Chester. (Cheers.) He had great pleasure in proposing "That this meeting is i of opinion that Mr. Geo. W. Latham s a fit and proper per- son to represent this division of Cheshire in Parliament, and pledges itself to use its best endeavours to secure his return. (Hear, hear, and loud cheering.) Mr. Clletimes REYNOLDS, J.P., who was heartily cheered, and greeted as "the only Liberal magistrate," seconded the resolution in a neat speech. The Hon. E. L. STANLEY, M.P., supported the resolution. He observed that one of the most important problems before the present Parliament was the question of the extension of the franchise, and there was no place where the need of that extension could be more keenly felt than in Runcorn. There was no doubt they were going to get the franchise there, because even their Tory opponents were beginning to dodge the question, and would not tell the people right out that they would vote against it. There were many signs that the question of the land laws was becoming a very attrac- tive one to the people, and there was no doubt that it would also be dealt with. But in order to have good legislation upon those questions we must have different men sent to Parliament. It was not right that the House of Commons should be thought to be the possession of the idle classes. We did not want the idle classes at all—(hear, hear,)—and it was to the existence of that idle class, which thought the country belonged to it, that we owed a good many of our national evils. (Applause.) It was not right that it should be thought that the representation of a county could be handed down from one member of a family to another, and that men of equal intelligence with those families should have no voice in the matter at all. (Applause.)

• Mr. T. SNAPB, who was cordially received, said he thought something more than building churches ought to be tajten into account in electing a representative. He could-not forget that iniquitous war, to which Mr. Latham I had alluded, in which that party that built churches was engaged, and he very much preferred that instead of build- ing churches, they would act in accordance with the way in which they were taught to act in the book which was read on Sundays in those churches. (Cheers.) Whatever might be Mr. Egerton's religious views, he did not believe from all he had heard him express, that he was disposed to carry out that golden rule which lay at the very foundation of all true religious faith, of doing unto others as he would that men should do unto him. (Cheers.) Had the Conservative party done so? ("No.") They knew the jubilation

they gave expression to in conneelon with the wars mere than once. He was reminded of that satirical verse, which Punch expressed and put into the mouth of the Emperor of Germany in the Franco-liernian war, when he wrote home to his wife :

My et:11-esi love, my own Agusta, To--day we've had dreadful buster; thousand Frenchmen sent 13., low, Praise God from whom all blessings flow. (Loud laughter.) That seemed to be the spirit in which so many of these clergymen, and so many God-fearing Con- servatives acted with reference to the wars in which they plunged the nation. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Snape attributed the slow progress which legislation had made, and the slow re- covery of trade to the wars promoted by the Conservatives, and speaking of land reform, advocated security for unex- hausted improvements, and related instances where tenant farmers' rents had been increased on their own improvements. He effectively ridiculed the Agricultaral Holdings Act passed by the Tories in 1875. Alluding to the proposed Affirmation Bill, he said it was a constitutional question. What was the true principle of the Constitution about which the Conservatives were so ready to utter unmeaning plati- tudes, and which they were so ready to desert upon oc- casions like this? The CoQtitution provided that every constituency should decide who should represent it in the House of Commons, with this qualification that the representative shall not be a felon. Mr. Bradlaugh was not a felon, and he was, therefore, en- titled to sit for the constituency which had appointed him. (Cheers.) It was the duty of the electors of Mid-Cheshire to send to Parliament a gentleman who would preserve the Constitution (cheers), and he believed the hour had come and with the hour had come the man, in the person of Mr. Latham. (Cheers). It would be for them on Wednesday next to show by their votes that with the hour and the man, victory had come as wall. (Cheers). The resolution was then carried with the greatest enthu- siasm, only about five persons, amongst whom was a lady, dissenting.

Mr. LiTILLM' who was greeted with an ovation briefly replied, and in doing so, proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, to whom he paid a high compliment for his earnest and valuable labours in the Liberal cause.
Mr. STANLEY, M.P., seconded the motion, which was car- ried with acclamation.
The meeting then separated. MR. LATHAM AT WARRINGTON.

A meeting of the electors in the Grappenhall polling dis- trict was held in the Public Hall, Warrington, on Wednes- day afternoon. There was a large attendance. Mr. C. Broadbent presided, and there were also present Mr. G. W. Latham, M.P., Mr. W. Summers, M.P., Mr. J. E. Johnson Ferguson, M.A. (Kenyon) Mr. W. Milne (Bowdon), Mr. Lloyd (Knutsford), Councillor Monks, Councillor Platt, Jac. Mr. H. ROBERTS read a letter of apology for non-attend- ance from Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., who wrote: "If I had been in Warrington I would have gladly attended your meeting in support of Mr. Latham on Wednesday. His presence in the House of Commons will be very valuable, considering his knowledge of the Land Question in Eng- land, which will probably receive more than usual attention this session. He knows as well as any man the laws and customs affecting the tenancy of land which prevent its proper cultivation, and which, as long as they continue, will interfere fatally with the prosperity of the tenant and the real interests of the landlord. If the farmers of Cheshire knew their own interests they will send Mr. Latham to Par- liament." Letters of apology had also been received from Mr. C. J. Morris and Mr. Z. Armitage. The CHAIRMAN said they had met there to supt.Ort Mr. Latham, and he did not think that there could be any meet- ing of a political character more than the present. Most of them were thorough going Liberals, and would be willing to return any man to Parliament who would be a supporter of the present Government, and especially the great man who had just returned from the Continent—(cheers)—to pursue his work in England. They would gladly support any can- didate who would support that Government and wished to carry out the business of the country, and not obstruct it. He was glad to think that there might be many there who were not what might be called ardent politicians, but went to hear both candidates and then decide which was the best for those interested in laud culture of England. It was on this peculiar ground, as well as because Mr. Laham was a good Liberal that they appealed to those interested in agriculture to support him. If there was any man living who thoroughly understood the land question it was Mr. Latham, now before them. (Cheers.) That question was the greatest at present, and most likely to prominently come before the House of Commons both in the present and in the coming session, and it was important that they should have a man as member of Parliament thoroughly understanding those things. (Hear, hear.) He N entured to think that Mr. Latham's good training, his in- terest in the land, and the fact of his being a farmer, fitted him to represent the division. (Cheers.) It fitted him better than having a seat in the Metropolitan Board of Works. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) Not that he wished to disparage Mr. Egerton's position on that Board—it spoke well for him that be was devoting himself to public work— but Mr. Latham's training and cultivation in Mid-Cheshire were better for them than .being a member ot the Metro- politan Board of Works. (Hear, hear.) He had pleasure in introducing the candidate. Mr. LATmear, who was most heartily received, remarked that the Hon. Alan Egerton, in the speech which he delivered at Sale the previous night, said he would be glad to know, seeing that Mr. Latham expressed himself in favour of tenant right, why he did not give tenant right to his own tenants. He (Mr. Latham) hated talking about himself, but, in reply-to Mr. Egerton's invitation, he would tell them what the agreement was which every tenant on his small estate might have if he liked. That agreement provided that every tenant should have two years' notice to quit—(hear, hear)—and have full compensation for unexhausted provemeuts. (Applause.) The tenant might also cultivate the land as he liked—(renewed applause)—and might sell anything off that he liked. The only condition which he (Mr. Latham) imposed was, that when the tenant left the farm he should leave a specified quantity of land either in permanent grass, or else in grass seeds laid down in well- cleaned land of an .plar.oyed hear.)._ Those adopted, though they varied sometimes. For instance, he granted a farmer a lease the other day, and gave him those conditions with this addition, that if during the currency of the lease the tenant wished to leave he might assign his lease to any responsible person with capital whom he could find. (Applause.) Mr. Egerton or somebody else had asked what good the Farmers' Alliance had ever done. Well, the Alliance had not so far done anything-practical, except that it had called the attention of the country to various matters vitally affecting the interests of farmers. The Farmers' Alliance had prepared two bills, the first of which carried out solely the principle of sale. The following year they drafted a bill in which the principle of sale was retained, arbitration being suggested as an alternative. That bill Mr. Howard brought into the House of Commons, hoping that it would go before a select committee in comoany with the bills of Sir Thomas Acland and Mr. Chaplin ; but it could not go before the Select Committee until it had passed the second reading, and the bill was so carefully blocked that it could not reach that stage. There never had been a chance therefore of the ebill being considered by a Committee of the House of Commons. But the Alliance adopted the other day, at a meeting at which he (Mr. Lat- ham) was present, proposals which declared that the Go- vernment bill, when introduced into the House, would not be satisfactory unless it provided two things, the first of which was that every tenant should receive compensation for unexhausted improvements; and the second, that no sitting tenant should have his lent raised upon his own im- provements. (Applause.) Mr. Egerton had stated that he was in favour of legislation for giving compensation for unexhausted improvements, but he added that he would prefer the landlord should do it by agreement with the ten- ant. (Cries of" Oh.") No doubt every man in the room was in favour of people doing what was right, but he did not see that that was a reason why laws should not be passed for preventing wrong-doing. The fact was that under the present system of land tenure tenants were not safe, He (Mr Latham) was in favour of au agreement between landlord and tenant, but it was necessary to have legislation, not only in order-to be able to deal with those bad landlords, who could not be made to give agreements and who tried to take unfair advantage of the tenant whenever they could, but also in order to provide for those circumstances which would arise on the best managed estates, when things had to be done which were not contemplated whpn the agree- ment was first entered into. (Applause.) Under the cir- cumstances, therefore, he thought his proposal was far more to the advantage of tenants than was that of Mr. Egerton. (Renewed applause.) Moreover, it was necessary to secure compensation for unexhausted improvements, in order that capital might be made secure. One instance of what might be called fraud on the part of a landlord towards a tenant would shake the confidence of the whole of the tenants in the district, and prevent them from cu'ltivating their land and improving their farms to the extent they otherwise would. (Applause.)

Mr. W. DAR/325111Rn said he rose with very great plea- sure to move a resolution, stating that "In the opinion of this meeting Mr. Latham is a fit and proper person to re- present Mid-Cheshire in Parliament, and that it further pledges itself to use every effort to secure his triumphant return." It was not necessary for him to say very much in moving that resolution. Mr. Latham was well known, not only in Warrington but throughout Mid-Cheshire. He had now been before them for a good many years, and they knew him perfectly well, and that what he said he would carry out. (Hear, hear.) He as an agriculturist supported the candidature of Mr. Latham, because he was to aid on a bill to give compensation for unexhausted manures and im- provements. That was a most important thing to tenant farmers. They knew that before now they had made improvements and expended money on manures to put on the land, and some of them had had to leave it behind them. Nothing would satisfy him, and the tenant farmers generally save that whatever they had expended in the shape of manure and improvements should be as sure of return as if it were placed in the bank. (Cheers.) When they could get that they could farm with confidence, and could better hold their own against foreign competition than at the present time. • Another reason for his support was be- cause Mr. Latham would forward a measure providing that a tenant's rent should not be raised upon his own improve- ments. It had been the custom frequently in Cheshire wher a tenant put a great many improvements on his farm that by-and-bye the landlord would notify him that if he would not give more rent some- one else would. (" Shame.") The consequence was that the tenant had to pay an advanced rent upon his own im- provements. Mr. Latham said he would try and prevent I that, and he would carry it out. (Cheers.) Some people

Iseemed to think that they were all alike at election times, and -would promise anything to get into Parliament, that one wa‘g as good as the other, and such like remarks. He might tell' them that he had the utmost confidence in Mr. Latham can,ving out the promises which he made before Ong to Peril& naent. (Hear, hear.) He was glad that Mr. Latham was in favour of the abolition of the law of distraint; that was ,that he would be in favour of the ordinary creditors of ti farmer, if he was so unfortunate as to become bankrupt, oring alike with the landlord, e or rather, that the landlord Ib9uld share alike with thet hrq other creditors. Wear, hear.) . had suffered very much himself from the present law, and ehould rejoice to see. ed. it abolished and something else oubstitues. It was not very long since that a landlord took all that a tenant owed in the shape of rent, which was some thre;:' years back. He (the speaker) happened rmfortunately ie, be the creditor, and he had to ber content with 10,1 in the pound. de considered that the landlord, who was ,7aid in full, was quite as able to lose his rent ale the credi..`°r his money. (Hear, hear.) They had now an opportunity of returning a gentleman to Parliament in whom they had the greatest confidence, and he hoped that during the week they would hear of his return to Parliament. To those electors who did not place very much importance upon their votes, for there were several he had come across who said "they would vote for the winning horse," he said they might take it that Mr. Latham would be the winner. (Laeghter and hear, hear.) He hoped that those gentlemen who only voted for the " winning horse" wonld vote for Mr. Latham. He thought they could not do better than do what the reso- lution said—use every effort to secure their candidate's triumphant return. (Cheers.) With regard to Mr. Eger- ton, the only claim which he had upon the electors of Mid-Cheshire was a hereditary one. (A. voice: " The accident of an aceident," and hear, hear.) They did not know Mr- Egerton until within the last week or two. He himself had never seen nor heard of him before, and he was only there because ute n'me was Egerton. (Hear, hear.) That would not satisfy him as an eteeter. He respec- ted the Egerton family very m udla indeed. He woula eeepect his own brother very much, but if he did not agree with his brother's sentiments he should net vote for him. (Cheers.) He asked them to vote for the gentleman whom they knew and had tried, and who had done more for the tenant farmers during the las ten years than all the Cheshire members put together, thought not a member of Parliament. (Loud cheers.) But give him an opportunity of distinguishing himself in the House of Commons, and he would do more than he had ever done before. (Renewed cheers.) Mr. BRADFORD, Redish Hall, seconded the resolution. The longer be knew Mr. Lathatn the better he liked him. He hoped they would give him all their votes, and thus enable him to win. (Cheers.) Mr. J. E. JOHNSON FERGUSON supported the resolution. He came there partly as a representative of the South-West Lancashire Liberal Asscciation and partly as a Scotch land- lord to tell them of the interest which was being taken in that election, and they urged upon them as electors of Mid- Cheshire to return Mr. Latham as a supporter of one of the best and strongest Governments that this country had known for years. (Cheers.) Why was it that the Govern- ment was powerful and popular to-day? Why was it that after three years' service it was more popular than when it entered into power? Sir Richard Cross had told them that that popularity was owing to the success in the Egyptian war. (A Voice: "So it is.") He did not think so, but it would not be an improper cause for popularity. (Hear, bear.) He thought that it was based on something sounder and better, and was that the country recognised the importance of that great series of important and useful reforms of which Mr. Latharn had mentioned two or three. (Hear, hear.) We had tried a Conservative Gcvernment, and found it incapable of dealing with those reforms. (Cheers.) During the three years that the present Government bad been ii . power, they had shown themselves able and willing to deal with those matters, and that great obstacle obstruction, which had been made SD much of by the last Government, had been ably and firmly grappled with by the present one. They were not only willing but determined to deal with those questions, which as Englishmen and Liberals they would like to see carried out. (Cheers.) One question to which Mr. Latham had not referred, was the power which at present existed for tying up land. No one could do his duty by the land when it was so disposed by law that he could not do at all what he otherwise would do. (Hear, hear.) The matter called for great attention, and he hoped that although concessions had been made in that direction the party would never rest until the land was free. (Applause.) Questions were invited, but only one was sent up inquiring if Mr. Latham would support the Manchester Ship Canal scheme. (Laughter.) Mr. LATHAM said he was much in favour of the cheap- ness of water carriage and also believed that it was a good thing to have competition between railways and canals, but he did not know the details of the scheme and should be sorry to pledge himself to anything of which he was not fully informed. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was put to the meeting and a large number of hands were held up in favour. On the contrary being put three or four bands were shown and were immediately greeted with cries "They have no votes " and derisive laughter. The resolution was then declared carried.

Mr. W. SUMMERS M.P., had great pleasure in asking them to support Mr. Latham for a great variety of reasons. Taken man for man, Latham and Egellon, he thought that Mr. Latham took the palm. He had lived in the county for some thirty years, he knew the interests of the county better than any man living, and though he had read the address of Mr. Alan Egerton, and all the speeches he had delivered, he must confess he had been unable to see in them any great evidence that Mr. Egerton had studied political mat- ters or had an intimate acquaintance with political matters. Mr. Latham represented the principles identified with the Liberal party; and it was because he was a great supporter of the present Government, it was because he would always be found voting in the right lobby on behalf of these great Liberal principles to which we owed the greatness of our country that he thought it would be a national benefit for Mr. Latham to be at the head of the poll on Wednesday next. .....,Tht..flues.tion bs, dfisllleCe9ex;ioFecNfa- fidence in Her Majesty's Administration? (Cheers.) He trusted they would show their belief in the present Government was greater than it was at the last election, and that Mr. Latham would not have a minority of 326, as was the case at the last election, but would have a majority of that, or a great number. (Cheers.) In his humble judg- ment Mr. Gladstone had been faithful to the pledges he gave in the great electioneering campaign of 1880; and he asked the electors to give their votes for Mr. Latham because he would support the Government in carrying out these great and important measures of reform which Mr. Gladstone's Government were as anxious as anybody could possibly be to carry into law at the earliest practicable moment. (Cheers.) He seconded the vote of thanks.
The vote of thanks having been carried, the CHAIRMAN briefly replied, and the meeting terminated.
SANDBACH.

A large meeting in support of Mr. Latham, the Liberal candidate, was held at Sandbach, on Thursday night. Mr. LATHAM, who was accorded an enthusiastic reception, called attention to the omission in his opponent's aoldress of any mention of a matter which affected Mid-Cheshire more than any other constituency for the reason that there was no Paz liamentary borough in the division—namtly, the equali- sation of the franchise. The present system was so absurd that he would not argue it. Mr. Egerton, his opponent, talked about a pro rata franchise, but he afterwards admitted that he was thinking about something else—the redistribution of seats. (Laughter.) A man whose ideas were so confused was not worthy of the suffrages of any body of electors. Referring to Irish affairs, Mr. Egerton had charged the Government with being morally guilty of the assassination of Lord Frederick Cavendish, which was not intended by the assassins. If anyone besides the criininals were to be blamed for the Dublin murders it was the House of Lords, who rejected the Bill for the reduction of rents of the people because they were unable to pay them. Mr. HOWAILID, MP., urged the electors to return Mr. Latham, to encourage one of the best Governments that had ever existed. His presence would be most helpful in Par- haircut, when so. many subjects affecting farmers were up for discussion and settlement. The question of agricultural reform had been taken up by the Government, and if it was not settled on rigid lines and in the right way a generation might lapse before the mistakes were rectified.—Mr. James TONICINSON, the Liberal candidate for West Cheshire, also spoke, and a motion of confidence was carried.

div.head: GREAT LIBERAL MEETING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: GREAT LIBERAL MEETING AT RUNCORN.

On Tuesday evening, a meeting was held in Runcorn Public Hall in support of Mr. G. W. Latham, the Liberal candidate. It was announced to commence at half-past seven, but half an hour before that time the room was almost filled, and when Mr. Shaw rose to address the meeting, the gallery and the body of the hall were crowded. At the commencement the proceedings seemed likely to be of a rather uproarious character, but they passed off quietly and harmoniously, and were characterised by the greatest enthusiasm, Mr. Robert Shaw, president of the Runcorn Liberal Association, occupied the chair, and amongst those present on the plat- form were—Mr. G. W. Latham, the candidate, the Hon. E. Lyulph Stanley, M.P. for Oldham, Mr. W. Woodall, M.P. for Stoke-on-Trent; the Revs. J. D. Thomas, George Hack, Sydney Mees, E. Williams, John Jones, Joseph Pickwell ; Messrs. C. H. Murray (United Kingdom Alliance), William Milne (chairman of the Liberal Executive Committee), T. Snape (Widnes), John Simpson, Charles Reynolds, J.P., S. C. Beckett, T. Norman, F. Fairhurst, W. Handley, James Handley, J. R. Frith, B. Kniveton, J. Littkr, F. Beck, Philip Speakman, Fred Rigby, Taylor, W. F. Pankhurst (London) and Oliver Leak (secretary). The CHAIRMAN, who was received with cheering, said it was about 11 years since Mr. Latham came befcre them as a candidate for the suffrages of Mid-Cheshire. Since that time they had been working for what they believed to be their rights—(eheers)—they had been endeavouring to get those who were not represented that day the means of re- presentation. (Hear, hear.) For about forty years Mid. Cheshire had been represented by two Tory members— (hisses)—who had done rothing whatever—(hear, hear)— to give a vote to intelligent men who were paying their fair share of the taxation of the country, and therefore had a right to that representation which others enjoyed. (Cheers.) He urged them to see clearly what were the issues of this contest, and asked what did Alan Egerton promise the voters of Mid-Cheshire. [A voice: Nothing. (Laughter and cheers.)] There never could have been a truer answer to that ques- tion. (Cheers.) The only thing that Mr. Egerton promised was that he would not oppose. He (Mr. Shaw) wanted to know whether in the 19th century men of intelligence were to be represented by those who had formed no opinions. In his address Mr. Latham had stated clearly his views on various important questions, and he (Mr. Shaw) hoped that the electors of Mid-Cheshire would do their utmost to return Mr. Latham on Wednesday next as member of Parliament, who would not only legislate for those who had given his votes to him, but also assist those who had no power to vote, but who ought to have a voice in the management of the country's affairs. (Cheers.)

Mr. WILLIAM Mulls said that day the Livopool Clourier —(hisses)—had given an account of a meeting held in that neighbourhood on the previous day, at which a speech was made !by the Vicar of Runcorn, whom he had not the pleasure of knowing. (Loud groans and cheers.) The TiCar of Runcorn asked those who heard him to vote for Mr. Egerton, because the latter's father had built a chnrch. (Hear, hear, laughter. and " no.") He (Mr. Milne) had several times visited Mr Latham on his estate; and the last time he was there he saw a Wesleyan chapel, the foundation stone of which was laid by Mrs. iLatham, and the ground upon which it was built was given by Mr. Latham to the Wesleyan denomination. (Great cheering). Knowing that Mr. Latham was a Churchman, he observed to himself that surely that gentleman had given something to the Church.(Uproar, and a Voice: "Turn him our.) He was tom that of course Mr. Latham gave land for a cburch too. (Cheers.) He was not there to bandy personalities; but he wished to know whether Lord Egerton ever gave any land ,to a Nonconformist place of worship. (Oheers and groans.) He knew for a fact that the friends of a little mission station with which he (the speaker) was connected in Mobberley, and on the very verge of Lord Egerton's principal estate, after having held cottage meetings there for years, wanted to build a school chapel, from which they tried to purchase land from his lordship, but he would not sell them it. (Loud groans.) He Should not have mentioned that fact in Runcorn, if the vicar of the parish had not made the remark to which he had referred. (Cheers and uproar.) Referring to the Rey. Wm. div.head: MEETINGS OF MR. EGERTON'S SUPPORTERS. ALTRINCHAM.
div.p: MEETINGS OF MR. EGERTON'S SUPPORTERS. ALTRINCHAM.

The Hon. Alan Egerton addressed a meeting of his sup- porters at Altrincharn, the headquarters of his opponent, Mr. Latham' last (Friday) evening week. Mr. Egerton explained in detail the views expressed in his address. He feared the County Boards Bill will prove of limited service to the coun- try in consequence of its centralising tendency, though in some respects the principle is good. A vote of confidence was carried.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

The Hon. Alan Egerton addressing a meeting at Lymin on Saturday evening propounded some views on the franchise which carry one back to Mr. Disraeli's " fancy franchise" proposals. Mr. Egerton "was in favour of every man who. was properly qualified by knowledge and by being able to exercise discretion having a vote, but it must be pro rata. Was property and was intellect to have no ad- vantage in voting ?" The Hon. E Stanhope, M.P., was able to say, after the experience of the debate on the Address, that "the Government had gagged their opponents." They had, he said, an overwhelming majority, and there would be no excuse if they did not give to the agricultural community that which it had a right to de- mand. Mr. Stanhope does not appear to have defined very clearly what relief he would give to the farmers, with the exception of some change in the incidence of local taxa- tion.

MOBBERLEY. The Conservative candidate, the Hon. Alan de Tatton I3,4erton, was favourably received at a meeting held in his support at Mobberley, on Monday. Mr. W. J. Harter, of Mobberley Hall—a magistrate for the county—who occu- pied the chair, delivered a speech which, it may safely be xssumed, will damage rather than promote Mr. Egerton's tndidature. To say that the Government is endeavouring 'o rule Ireland "by a policy of cutting off cows' tails" is in expression hardly to be expected even from a Tory !leetion speaker. The rector of the parish, not content viLh attending the meeting, caused the church bells to bc ang in honour of the candidate's visit,

frave great pleasure in directing attention to the subjoined. announcement, and while thanking their eustc,mers for much generous support in the past, respectfully solimi for the new Company a continuance of the patronage worded to the old firm.
JOHN CAMMACK AND COMPANY, LIMITED,
INCORPORATED FEBRUARY,., 1883.
CAPITAL, 45,000 IN SHABES OF 41 EACH.
DIRECTORS :
MR. JAMES GANDY, CHAIRMAN, MR. JAMES MACKAY, MR. JOHN DONNELLY.
MANAGING DIRECTOR;
MR. JOHN CAIIMAOK, F.I,C.
SECRETARY:
MR. JOHN W. PICKTON.

The yearly increasing demand for non-intoxicant beverages has compelled Messrs. J. Cammack and Co. to meet it by the infusion of new blood and additional capital into the firm; hence the formation of the present company. The directors enter on th jr office with the determination to give every pos- sible satisfaction to their patrons, and to make the company second to no firm in the kingdom, whether in the excellence of its beverages, the moderation of its prices, or the careful atten- tion of its officers to the wants of customers.

The consumption of rlneral and Aerated Waters has grown sa rapidly that a keen competition in their supply has been excited, resulting in the introduction of some very unsound and even poisonous beverages.

This degeneracy has arisen partly through the incapacity of the old rule-o'-thumb manufacturers, vrho still maintain their antiquated apparatus, consisting of copper vessels, whose tin lining, if they ever had any, has long since beeu removed, and common lead piping—sure and ferthe sources of poisonous metalic contamination—and partly through the greed and rapacity of the modern but not less ignorant speculators in the business, who, descending to the vilest, because cheapest means of production, use defective seemd-hand machinery; and employ impure and often poisonous ingredients in the nnrrinnaitinr, tuokti. the goods are supplied has not escaped the effects of this cupidity, for the small wooden stopper adopted in the cheapest type of patent bottle in common use, instead of being weighted with pure block tin is frequently found loaded with lead, the most dangerous metal for such a purpose, as it is well known to be a virulent and an accumulative poison.

The proper choice and erection of machinery and apparatus; the adoption of suitable precautionary measures during the process of manufacture, the ability to seleet and the power to make or purify the various ingredients, absolutely require the experience and knowledge of a trained Chemist. His active and unremitting personal supervision is also needed to avoid or destroy the various noxious ferments which are so apt to form, and the myriads of organised germs, cells, bacteria, &c., which are now admitted to be a frequent source of disease, and gym death.

The Directors are therefore pleased to have retained the pro- fessional services of Mr. John Cammack (Fellow of the Insti- tute of Chemistry and of the Society of Chemical Industry), as Managing DirePtor, whose name is so well and honourably known in the district of St. Helens, and whose long and varied experience in Scientific and Technical hemistry will be sure guara...tee of the purity and excellence of the Various btverages.

Itc,reover, they have adopted nasehinery and apparatus of the latest and most improved type. Every portion of it which comes into actual contact with the Aerated Waters and the Syrups is constructed of glass, porcelain, pure block tin, or tg real gun metal (not corrodable brass) thickly lined with I^_are block tin. Lead is entirely discarded, even the solder used in making the various connections being free from that noxious metal.

For the storage of the Solutions and Syrups, only slate. earthenware, or glass 'vessels are used, wood being entirely dis- pensed with as too absorbent and retentive of foul flavours ant! Energetic ferments.
All the Waters and Syrups are carefully filtered before being used.
A special apparatus is employed to thoroughly rinse even the last traces of the wash water from the bottles.
The Sweet Drinks are composed of none but real fruits essences and extracts and harmless vegetable compounds.

The Mineral Waters contain the purest materials, anti are guaranteed strength. The SODA WATER, which is UNEXZELL by any other manufacturers, contains the standard quantity carbonate of soda, and is not, like the rubbish too often su plied, plain water indifferently carbonated.
All the Patent Bottles used are stoppered with glass, and the Corked Goods are of a Special and Superior Quality.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- SIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Board Room on Wednesday, under the chairmanship of Dr. Steele. There were also present—Dr. McDougall, Messrs. T. Norman, R. Shaw, Taylor, Rhodes, Pritchard, Williams, Meadowcroft, F. A. Lake, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), and W. Brookes (secretary).

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical Officer's monthly report stated that during February there had been 29 deaths registered in Runcorn and 2 in Halton-within-Runcorn, while 5 inquests had been held, making the total deaths 36, which represented a death rate of 24 per 1,000 per annum. Fifteen deaths occurred among children five years and under, and four under one year. Pulmonary diseases accounted for 13 deaths, scarla- tina 5, and natural decay 4.

UPPER BIBRSEY NAvu-smrsovr. A. letter was read from Mr. Collier intimating that Mr. Charles Wigg's appointment as a member on the Mersey Navigation Commissioners had expired, and on the motion of Mr. NortarArr, seconded by Mr. TAYLOR, Mr. Wigg was re-appointed.

div.head: 'THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: 'THE SHIP CANAL.

The CHAIRMAN intitnated that it was time the Board should take some steps with regard to the Manchester Ship Canal.—Mr. SHAW observed that the Board did not need to take any steps at all. The scheme, as it now stood, did not effect Runcorn in the least, and the promoters would have to deposit plans before they could interfere with the river.—lt was stated that the scheme would interfere with the sewerage of the town, but Mr. Nor- man declared that this was not a fact.—The SURVEYOR said that the canal would interfere with three of the Board's outlets.—Mr. NORMAN remarked that the Canal Company would hive to make good anything they came in contact with. —Mr. SHAW said tbroagh the law clerk occupying a double position, he was sorry to say he was trying to force the Board. He was interested in the promotion of the scheme—(The LAW CLERIC: He is not)— as well as looking after the Commissioners' interest, and be- fore the Board was asked to have a meeting of the kind proposed, somebody ought to show that the.canal scheme would really interfere with the rights of the people of Run- corn.—Mr. MEADOWCROFT agreed with the remarks of Mr. Shaw.—The CHAIRMAN said he only mentioned the matter as chairman of the Board.—Mr. Snew said the promoters could not stop up the drains if they purchased the canal without buying the right to do so.—The LAW CLERK ob- served that the Act asked for power to acquire certain drains and outfalls within a line of the canal.—The matter then dropped.

div.head: QUESTIONED RIGHT TO VOTE.
div.p: A QUESTIONED RIGHT TO VOTE.

. - On the minutes of the last meeting of the Board being read, Mr. NORMAN said he wished to draw the attention of Chairman to the fact that Mr. Whitaker had no right to vote on the question respecting the Gas Company. —The CHAIRMAN : I intend at the close of this meeting to give notice of a resolution to be discussed at the next meeting on the subject. Idoso on the ground that, being a director, in courtesy, it was not right to do it.

div.head: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee contained a resolution instructing the Surveyor to serve notices on the owners of cottage property in Back Cooper-street to have the property put in a better sanitary condition, and on Major Orred's agent to improve the sanitary condition of farm premises at Higher Runcorn and premises in High-street.— On March Ist a letter was read from the Mersey Salt and Brine Company, Limited, asking permission, after testing their reservoir, to run the "'Ater into the sewer in Mough- lands-road. Recommendation, that the surveyor reply that on the company giving an undertaking that within one month they will put in proper repair the road learing from Heath-road to the Rifle Butts, damaged by their contractors, or repay to the Commissioners such sum as they themselves may expend in such repairs to the satisfaction of the sur- veyor., the permission asked for be granted, the surveyor to have the oversight, and all damage to be made good. —The minutes were adopted on the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. WILLIAMS

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The minutes of the Canal Boats and Hospital Committee, who recommended that £75 be paid Mr. Statham on account of hospital contract, were adopted on the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. TAYLOR.—The Finance Com- mittee reported that the receipts for February amounted to £3ll 145., and accounts amounting to £242 163. 54. were recommenied for payment. Passed on the proposal of Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN. WATERLOO BRIDGE. IMPROVEMENTS TO BE MADE.

Dr. MACDOUGALL proposed "That the Commissioners having purchased land and prepared plans for improving and widening Waterloo Bridge 9 and the approaches thereto; and also having in hand since 1878 sufficient funds to cover the cost, it is expedient for the public convenience and safety that the work be carried out forthwith." The Doctor reviewed all the proceedings which the Board had taken in reference to this matter since March sth, 1877, when it was first mooted by a petition from the residents at Top Locks. He said he thought the present time opportune for again raising the question inasmuch as the Board had in hand ,ei,eod 4- .4,, ,vnrl,--an amount which the Surveyor had said would be ample to make the bridge into What it really ought to be. The traffic upon the bridge was constantly increasing, while the roadway had become absolutely dangerous to pedestrians, and the money could not be devoted to a better purpose than repairing the bridge. He, therefore, with confidence asked the Board to adopt the resolution he had proposed.— Mr. SHAW seconded the resolution in the interest of the trade of the town. It must be clear to every Commissioner that the bridge was used for heavy traffic very much more than Savage's Bridge, because the gradient of the latter was too steep. They would find that the bulk of the traffic, which was constantly increasing, between the railway and the town went over Waterloo Bridge, and if they were to do any good to the town, it must be by giving increased facili- ties to the tradespeople.—Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN inquired if the bridge was private property.—The LAw CLERK replied in the negative. There was a road there before the bridge was erected. If it were private property the Bridgewater Navigation Company weuld have a right to close it up.— The CHAIRMAN, in moving an amendment, said his reason for doing so was not to prevent alteration to the bridge, be- cause it was dangerous, but there were more dangerous spots in the town--Lee's corner in High-street for instance. He moved an amendment to the effect "That inasmuch as the Bridgewater Trustees, in their agreement dated 16th August, 1867, reserve themselves the power from time to time, and at any time hereafter, to alter, repair, and amend the fabric of Waterloo Bridge and, the approaches thereto, they be asked to widen the bridge or throw over the canal a light bridge to be used as a footpath, the Commissioners undertaking to keep the surface of such bridge in repair."— The Likw CLERK said as the Board had a conveyance of land from the Bridgewater Navigation Co. for the purpose of doing certain work, and there was a plan upon that deed and coanterpart showing what had to be'done, it did not look business like to enter into the Chairman's proposal 1:101V.-Mr. SHAW: 'lt is childish.—Mr. j. J. SPEAKMAN seconded the propesition.—Mr. SHAW aiaed the chairman to withdraw this amendment. The Board ought to endeavour to conduct its buisness like business men. After the Board had rightly'or wrongly gone the lenght it had to ask the Bridgewater Company to do what they were not obliged to do seemed to him very childish. He would not be a party to putting the Board in that undignified position. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. LAKE gave his opinion that the clause read by Dr. Steele was to protect the company's traffic underneath the bridge.—Dr. MacDouaAer, replied, observing that the proceedings in connection with Waterloo Bridge was a reflection upon the business capacity of the Board.—The amendment was then put and lost, when the CHAIRMAN said that was what he had expected, and he therefore pro- posed another amendment, as fellows :—" That a copy of the agreement with the Bridgewater Trustees, dated IGth August, 1867, with an explanation as to why the agreement was made be sent to the Local Government Board, and their consent obtained before any alterations is made to Waterloo Bridge.—The LAW CLERK remarked that the chairman was making a precedent for the interference of the Local Government Board, which might be very irksome in the future; he was asking them to assume a position which they did not possess—(hear, hear); and which they would claim as a precedent —After a little conversation, the CHAIRMAN withdrew the amendment, which he said he proposed to keep himself and the public right. —The orig;nal motion was then passed, and Messrs. Lake, Pritchard, Rhodes, Shaw, and MacDougall were appointed a cAmMittee to obtain competitive plans and estimates.
