div.head: EAAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 10, 1883.
div.p: THE EAAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 10, 1883.
RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr.W. Wynne-yfoulkes, Judge..

FousnAw T. Wain AND A CTON.—In this case, which was an action to recover £l4, value of a horse killed through the alleged negligence of the defendants.—Mr. Fletcher, who was instructed for the defence, made an application to have the action struck out as against the defendant Weir, who was found on Monday last shot through the body by the acci- dental discharge of a gun be was using. Mr. Fletcher quoted authorities to show that in a case of the present kind the action could not proceed against the representatives of the deceased, but his Honour, after hearing Mr. Burton for the plaintiff, agreed to adjourn the case to the following court.

LEWIS V. SPENDER: HAGGLING OVER THE HtRDLEs In this case, which was a claim for £I2 for repairs dose to some hera lee belenGeeg ca the defendant, a farmer, formerly ot Sutton, but now of Blackford, near Chester. Mr. Flet- cher appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Hitchen for the de- fendant.—Mr. Fletcher, in opening the case, said, that in the early part of January last year the plaintiff saw the de- fendant at his farm. A conversation took place between them and the defendant told the plaintiff he had some hurdles that wanted repairing, and showed him some which were then in the yard, saying that there was about 120 up and down the f _rm, but they were not in so bad a condition as the numb: he saw, and he supposed he would repair them for sixpence a piece. The plaintiff considered he was only joking, and said" no ; but if you send them to tke smithy I will do them." The hurdles were sent and the plaintiff commenced to repair them. One day as the defendant was passing the plaintiff's smithy, the plaintiff called him and shewed him 20 hurdles which he had repaired, and asked. him if they were satisfactory. The defendant said " they look as good as new, but don't charge me new price for them."— Nothing further took place,anethe plaintiff repaired the lote A bill was afterwards sent in for the amount, but no notice taken of it, and the plaintiff afterwards went and saw th- defendant at his place and gave him a second bill. The dee fendant then said that his bargain was 6d. a piece and hd would pay no more. The plaintiff denied this, and refusee to take that sum, and entered the case in court.—The plaintiff bore out the statement of Mr. Fletcher, and in r- ply to Mr. Hitchen, said the usual charge for repairing hurdles of this description was 23 to 23 6d. It was,impos- sible to do them for less.—H. Bell and George Spender, two workmen of plaintiff's, Frederick Edwards, farm bailiff, formerly on the Aston Estate, corroborated the plaintiff's evidence as to it being impossible to repair the hurdles for 6tl each, the former saying that it took two men half an hour to take a hurdle to pieces before commencing to repair it. This concluded the plaintiff's case, and Mr. Hitchen called the defendant, Thomas Lewis, who stated that he remembered the plaintiff coming to his yard asking him if he had any work to do, to which he replied—No. Plaintiff said , What about those hurdles: They want doing? He replied I have some more on the farm, and we went together to look at them. I then asked him what he would do them for, to which he replied "Well, they ;don't seem to want much I doing at; I will take and do them for 6d each all round." Upon this the hurdles were sent to the smithy.—ln cross- I examination by Mr. Fletcher, defendant denied having said to plaintiff when he saw the 20 hurdles he had replied "that they were as good as new, but he must not charge a new price for them.—John Lewis and Samuel Worrell, workmen in the employ of the defendant, gave evidence.— A blacksmith, Upton, near Chester, said, in reply to Mr. Hitchen, that he had been in the business 40 years. It was not necessary to take a hurdle to pieces to repair either the bars or feet. He had repaired scores of hurdles, and never charged more than is. each.—The Judge, in summing up, said the evidence was very conflicting, and in cases of this kind he was bound by the weight of evidence brought before him. The defendant's statement was not corroborated, whilst that of the plaintiff was supported by several witnesses, and taking the whole of the evidence into con- sideration he must give judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed. A Cleavers FAMILY DlSPlTTE.—Thonacts Edwards and wife v. John Dutton and John Wright, executors of T'hos Cooper.—Mr. Hitchen appeared for the plaintiffs in this case, which was a claim for £3l 17s sd, value of goods detained, damages for detention, money lent, and money bad and received.—Mary Ann Edwards, one of the plaintiffs, in reply to Mr. Hitchen, said that previous to last November the late Thomas Copper (her brother) came to visit her fre- quently. On the 10th of November last she received a letter from her brother asking her to come and see him. She found him very ill. He said he had some furniture he wanted her to take care of, and mentioned several articles which were afterwards written upon a piece of paper by her son at her brother's dictation, and which her brother in- tended she should have at his decease. He took his watch and chain and placed it around her neck, saying, "Here, I'll give thee this, and no one can say thou has stolen it." He also asked Dutton, one of the defendants, to write him out an I 0 U for £5 which she had lent him in September pre- vious, but 9utton declined, saying that she or one of her family must do it. Her son afterwards wrote it out at her brother's dictation. She heard her brother say to her husband, "I've telegraphed to you to take these things away, go to the joiner's shop and get a man to come and take the things down," which he then enumerated to my husband. Her husband went, but the time and, in_coneeouence of what he said her husband was called back. During along cross-examination by Mr. Lake, who appeared for the de- fendants, the witness admitted that she had great power over he brother, and that they were always on affectionate terms. She also admitted that she gave him brandy during his illness, but it was upon the advice of the doctor. She gave him a tablespoonful of brandy and water as often as he asked for it. She never gave it to him "neat."—Thomas Edwards, husband of the previous witness, and one of the plaintiffs, gave evidence, as well as a son of the above.— Mr. Lake, for the defence, submitted that there were vir- tually three claims, viz., one in detinue, one for debt, and one for money had and received. As to the first—the claim to furniture—he submitted that it was either a gift inter vivos, op else donation mortis causa, and that in either case it was incomplete owing to non-delivery, and that it was in- complete owing to non-delivery, and that it was obtained by undue influence and coercion, and, as to the other items, that no case had been proved. He then called Dr. Bagnall, who said he was asked to exannine the plaintiff's brother the day before he died. From questions put to Cooper he considered that he was not rational, nor was he in a fit state to enter into any lengthened conversation, and his opinion was that besides general decay, he was suf- fering from the effects of too much stimulant. He appeared to be under the control of his sister.—Mrs. Cooper said that when her husband was ill, his sister came to see him and nursed him. Whilst she was there she treated the wit- ness more as a servant than as mistress of the house. Mrs. Edwards used to give her husband brandy frequently, some- times as much as half a glassful at a time without water. Her husband was always in the habit of paying for things as he bought them, and there was no necessity for him to borrow:any money.—At this stage of the case, it being half- past five, and there being several witnesses to call, the judge adjourned the. case to the next court day.

'o Liverpool and seized by the police in the same way.i After that be packed up at his brother's request other bales of goods. Two or three of them he took to Larry Rippell's house. He did not know who removed the others. After the liquidation he took Alexander Mackie, the trustee's bailiff, to tbe places in Widnes where the goods had been deposited. Further evidence in substantiation of Martin Connor's testimony was given by Mackie, the trustee's bailiff, and Mr. Price. P.C. Laing deposed to apprehending the debtor on the 27th February. The prisoner reserved his defence, and was committed for trial at the next Quarter Sessions, but admitted to bail in two sureties of .£lOO each.

(Continued from page 6.) MID-CHESHIRE ELECTION. FEELING IN RUNCORN. Both political parties have held a number of meetings in the neighbourhood of Runcorn during the past week, and from the nature of these gatherings some idea of the feelings of the electors on the question they are asked to decide may be inferred. The chances of success of the Liberal candi- date, it must be generally admitted, seem very bright, and his supporters are sanguine of returning him to St. Stephen's by a satisfactory, if not very large, majority. Runcorn, at all events, may be relied upon to support Mr. Latham by a majority of over a hundred. This is no hap- hazard guess, but a prediction founded upon an intimate knowledge of the political feeling in the district. Since the general election of 1881, the large towns in the division have had large additions to the electorate. In Runcorn polling district at that time the number of electors on the register was 740. There are now 876 electors, being an in- crease of 136, and a large proportion of these will, without doubt, exercise the franchise in favour of Mr. Latham. It is cmfidently believed that the " new" electors in the other towns are also to a great extent of Liberal principles, and if this be so, the advocate of land reform and the social amelioration of the labouring classes will inflict a decisive defeat upon the apostle of Tory obstruction and oppression. In consequence of Mr. Latham's views on the Licensing question, the Good Tem- plars of Runcorn have unanimously decided to support his candidature, which will be a further source of strength to the Liberal party. Through the utterances of two local Tory parsons at a meeting at Weston, on Menday evening, the contest in Runcorn has been made to assume a some- what personal character. The charges made against Mr. Latham were such as one would not have expected any person to make without careful inquiry, but reckless in- difference seemed to be the chief characteristic of the gentlemen who uttered them to a meeting which received the statements with severe eilence. It is satisfactory to know that their refutation was full and easy of accomplish- ment by Mr. Latham, who did not allow his detractors to escape scatheless. On Tuesday evening a second meeting to support the candidature of Mr. Latham will be held in the Public Hall, when Mr. William Summers, M.P. for Stalybridgc, anti other geotlernen will deliver spoechea. MR. LATHAM'S MEETINGS. MEETING AT RUNCORN LAST NIGHT. Last night a meeting, held with the object of further- ing the candidature of the Hon. Alan Egerton, the Con- servative candidate, took place in Runcorn Public Hall, under the presidency of Dr. Steele. There was a crowded audience, which contained many Liberals. On the plat- form were Sir Henry Holland, M.P., Mr. A. Pell, M.P., Mr. J. C. Lawrence, M.P., Rev. J. J. Bryant, M.A., Rev. W. Preston, M.A., Captain C. W. Hazlehurst, Dr. Mouritz, Messrs. Fisher, Rhodes, J. Ashton, Lightburn, J. J. Speakman, ttc. A number of letters of apology for non- attendance were read, amongst which was one from the Rev. Canon Barclay, who, referring to the speech of Mr. Latham, at Weston, on Tuesday, said there was not a particle of truth in the statement that he had had a quarrel with a clergyman at Weston Point. He thought a gentleman who talked of the lies of parsons should be care- ful of publicly uttering an untruth himself.— The Chairman and Mr. Egerton having delivered short speeches, Captain C. W. HAZLEIIIIRST briefly moved a re- solution of confidenae in the cmdidate.—Dr. MOURITZ seconded, and Sir HENRY HOLLAND, M.P. for Midhurst, supported the resolution. He remarked that the Govern- ment might have prevented the war in Egypt had the Go- vernment acted judiciously at the commencement of the affair, and declared that they had concluded a disgraceful peace in the Tranevaal. A reference to Mr. Latham and Mr. Gladstone was received with three cheers; and alluding to the Affirmation Bill, be said the question of Mr. Brad- laugh had not to be confounded with religious persecution, which was the curse of nations for four and five centuries. It was not a question of sect, or difference in religion. It was a question as to whether the House of Commons should allow a bridge to be built over the gulf between Atheism and religion. They must remember that the Tory party had prevented Mr. Bradlaugh from going through a farce of taking the oath in the House of Commons' and it was the duty of every religious sect to unite to keep Mr. Bradlaugh out of Parliament. —The Chairman neglected to put the resolution to the meeting, but called upon Mr. A. FELL, M.P., to move "That in the opinion of this meeting the present Government, by its conduct of Irish affairs, its foreign policy, and its domestic legislation, has forfeited the confi- dence of the nation, and is no longer worthy of support."— The resolution was seconded by Mr. T. MITFORD and sup- ported by Mr. J. A. LAWEANCE, M.P., JAMES ZOWRED, of Liverpool, and JOHN BROM—The CHAIRMAN now put the motion of confidence in Mr. Egerton to the meeting, and the latter one, when they were defeated by a considerable majority; but the Chairman declared, amid great laughter, that they had ben cartied:;unanimously.—Colonel TALBOT, amid cries of question, proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was carried, and the meeting broke up , amid cheering for Latham.

div.head: INSOLVENCY OF P. O'CONNOR,
div.p: THE INSOLVENCY OF P. O'CONNOR,
COMMITTAL OF THE DEBTOR.

At Prescot Police Court, on Friday, Patrick O'Connor was brought before Mr. Evans, charged under the sth sub- section of section 11 of the Debtors' Act, 1869, with having within four months, before the commencement of liquida- tion proceedings, fraudulently removed part of his property of the value of £lO or upwards. Mr. Stananought (Yates, Son, and Stananought, solicitors, Liverpool), prosecuted by instruction of the solicitor to the Treasury; the trustee of tho debtor's estate (Mr. Samuel Tilzey) was represented by Mr. H. L. Price' accountant to the Manchester Guardian Society, of which Mr. Tilzey is secretary; and Mr. F. Quelch, Liverpool, watched the case on behalf of the debtor.

Mr. Stananought, in opening the case, said that for four or five years the prisoner had carried on business as a tailor and draper in Waterloo Toad, Widnes. Up to October of last year he seemed to have been in rather a good position, having paid for all his stock. During October and Novem- ber he purchased stock to the amount of £4OO. In Decem- ber a creditor pressed him for a payment. Business did not appear to have been so good in the fall of the year, and on the 22nd December the prisoner filed a petition for the liquidation of his affairs by arrangement or composition. It had since been discovered that previous to the filing of the petition the prisoner had packed up and forwarded to Ireland three bales of cloth and a parcel of I,osiery, part of his stock-in-trade. Those goods arrived at Car- raduff, county Roscommon, on the 19th Decent Ger, and the petition was filed on tho 21st. On the 26th Decem- ber the debtor's stock was taken by Mr. Greaves, a prin- cipal creditor, and was found to amount to £330, while the debtor's liabilities were a few pounds over £4OO. After the stock-taking the debtor packed up and forwarded, through his brother, to Ireland some pictures, looking- glasses, and clocks. The goods were stopped by the Liverpool police, on the 13th January. The first meeting of creditors was held on the 161 h January, when a reso- lution was passed that the affairs of the debtor should be liquidated by arrangemenf,:and Mr. Samuel Tilzey, of Manchester, accountant, was appointed trustee. After the meeting of creditors, and before the trustee took posses- sion, on the 19th January, the debtor forwarded to Ire- land three or four bales of goods. Walter Ellis, assistant to the registrar of the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, having produced the file of the liquida-. tion proceedings,

Martin O'Connor, of Carraduff, county Roscommon, farm labourer, deposed that he was the debtor's brother. In De- cember last, the debtor wrote to him to come to his place of business at Widnes, and he did so. On the Tuesday before Christmas Day, acting under his brother's direction, he packed up and sent to his own address in Ireland one bale of cloth. He also took five or six bales to different houses in Widnes, but he could not say for sure how many bales were " shifted" from his brother's premises. He took four or five bales to a house in Pitt-street, where a man named named Larry Ilippell lived; one small bale to the house of a man named Featherstone; auother to the house of a pub- lican named Tansey ; and two others to the house of a man called Stafford. Besides the cloth thus disposed of, he packed in cases two clocks, ' three looking glasses and some pictures, and took them to the Clarence Dock, Liverpool, for shipment to Ireland, but they were taken possession of at the dock by the police. A small counter, a table, a step ladder, and a stool were taken i

div.head: WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.
div.p: THE WIDNES WOUNDING CASE.

Before Messrs. W. L. Evans and John Brock, at the Wid- nes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday; Thomas Quinn was brought up on remand, charged with unlawfully wounding John Clarke, on the 12th ult., with intent to do him grievous bodily harm.—John Clarke, labourer, deposed that on Monday, the 12th February, he lived at Thomas Cos- Lilo's, 44, Wellington-street, Widnes. On the morning of that day he went to his work as usual, and returned at nine o'clock. He remained in the house, where the prisoner Quinn also lodged. Quinn was in the house on the day in question. About three or four o'clock in the afternoon the prisoner asked him to go out and "have a drink with him," and he accornpanied him to an adjacent beerhouse, where the prisoner paid for three pints ot beer. Prosecutor had not then any money. On leaving the beerhouse, he went to Mr. Matthews, for whom he was working, and obtained some money from him. He subsequently returned to the beerhouse. The prisoner was not then there. The prisoner and he were good friends at this time. They remained at the beerhouse until about eight o'clock, and then returned to his lodgings. The prisoner and he then had supper together. No quarrel took place during the meal. After sapper a difference occurred between the prisoner and witness about some butter. Witness went to bed and prisoner followed him immediately, and then renewed the quarrel. Witness was standing up, and was undressed at the time. The prisoner said something in a threatening in inner, and Came towaids Lim. Witrica3 etru.3l.• at him to keep him away. Tue prisoner then took up an article of chamberware and btruck him with it on the head. The article was broken, and the force of the blow knocked him against the window, which he smashed, nearly fall- ing into the street. -He seized hold of the sill with his left hand or he would have fallen into the street. The force of the blow inflicted the injuries from which he had been suffering. He was attended by Dr. McLennan the same night, and was under his ca:e for several days, and was then removed to the hospital at Whiston Work- house, where he had been until that morning. The prisoner did no.t strike him with his fist after he had committed the first assault. He tried to strike him again, but he warded off the blow. He lost a great quantity of blood from the injury to his bead, and was still suffering from the effects of the assault.—Mary Costello, wife af Thomas Costello, 46, Wellington-street, Widnes, stated the last Witness and the prisoner lodged at her house on the 12th February last. They had supper there in the evening. After tea Clarke remarked that half a pound of butter had been used. Shortly afterwards the two men went to bed, and ten ; minutes after she heard the- noise of the window being I smashed. Subsequently both men came downstairs. Both were covered with blood.—Dr. McLennan said he attended the prosecutor, and found on the head an incised wound, three inchea iOI3Z, and penetrating to the bone. The wound was a clean one. There was a small artery cut, which, when he first examined it, was bleeding freely. There was a small indentation in the bone inside the wound. He found several pieces of pottery in the wound. The prosecutor could not have lived had not these been removed. The wound was a dangerous one.—The prisoner, who said he had nothing to say in defence, was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: ALLEGED OUTRAGE ON A GIRL AT
div.p: ALLEGED OUTRAGE ON A GIRL AT
WIDNES.

Before Mr. George Pilkington, and Mr. John Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Archibald Little, who described himself as a medical practitioner, and stated that he had studied at the Dublin Hospital, and who has for some months past vended patent medicine in Widnes market, was charged with committing a criminal assault on Martha Jane Hulme, a girl 14 years of age, whose parents live at 15, Luton-street.—The prosecutrix said "the doctor" (the Pri- soner) had been attending her mother's:baby, which eves suffering from the measles. He also attended other children. He was at her home on Sunday evening, and a little before eleven o'clock asked her to go with him to his house in Luton-street as he "could not see the door." She went with him, but they could not get into the house by either the front or the back door. The prisoner then dragged her into an entry, put his hand over her mouth, and crimi- nally assaulted her. At the expiration of five minutes they heard footsteps approaching, and her mother arrived on the scene. The prisoner then said, "We could not get in; the door was fast." She afterwards told her mother what had occurred.—Mrs. Hulme, the mother of the prosecutrix, atatad that the prisoner, who reported himself as a doctor, had been attending two of her children. who had been ill with the tneaale. for the past Six weeks. The prisoner went to her house on Sunday night, and remained in conversa- tion far nearly an how. nre.L h. Lo.a i.c. ah. e.;...a daughter, and becoming anxious she went out, and eventu- ally found the prisoner and her daughter standing near the prisoner's back gate. Her daughter was crying. Witness gave her a" smack" on the face, and asked her what she was doing there, but she made no reply, and ran home. Subsequently the father gave information to the police, and Dr. McLennan was called in. Her daughter had not been in the habit of going out at night. She was a quiet, steady, truthful girl—Dr. McLennan deposed to making an examination of the girl. He found she had been criminally assaulted.—P.S. Robinson deposed to apprehending prisoner, who, when formally charged, said, "I deny the whole accu- sation upon my oath. It gives me great consolation to be able to stand up and do so."—He was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
NANT WICK.

CONFIRMATION AT NANTWICII.-011 Wednesday, Bishop Kelly, acting for the Bishop of Chester, held a confirmation in Nantwich Church. Tbere were a large number of candi- dates, and the female candidates from Nantwich and Cop- penhall wore a substitute for caps, invented by the rector of the parish, which is simple and effective. In the latter parish they will he kept from year to year as church pro- perty. The Rev. E. A. Fitzroy, of St. Jude's, Liverpool, preaching on Tuesday night at Coppenhall, said that if every parish could present such a percentge of its parishioners for confirmation-67, of whom there were only' four more females than males, and 12 were elderly married men— there would be no fear for the good old Church of England. FRODSHAM.

LITERARY AND DEBATING SUDIETY.--On Monday even- ing a meeting of the above society was held in the Girl's School, Church-street, when Mr. Charles E. Linaker pre- sided, and there was a good attendance. The subject for debate was "Oliver Cromwell; does he merit our censure or approbation ?" and was introduced by Mr. Albert H. Walker in an excellent paper. On a show of hands being taken, a majority was declared in favour of the essayist, and the usual votes of thanks brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: IVINSFORD.
div.p: IVINSFORD.

Fttzs.—On Wednesday morning, the inhabitants of Wins- ford were startled by hearing the fire-bell ringing vigorously. It turned out that the old buildings at the top of Walsh- lane had by some means or other unknown got on fire. The only inhabitant, at the time, a calf, was got out, and in order to save the houses near—the wind blowing the flames in their direction—the engine was sent for, and was speedily there. In half an hour the flames were got under. The. damage is not serious. WINSFORD CIRCUIT —The quarterly meeting of the Winsford and Sandbach Circuit was held as usual at Mid- dlewich, the centre of the circuit. There was a good number of representatives present, and the business of the preachers' meeting having been transacted, the stewards' meeting was held. Financially the amount brought up was a few pounds below requirements; but, the error will speedily be rectified. The representatives appointed to next district meeting, to be held in Liverpool, are the Rev. W. T. ymons and Mr. J. Buckley. The plan committee are the two ministers, Rev. W. T. Symons, J. Wright, Messrs. Cooke, C. Allen, T. Oakes and Hodkins. The consolidation of the circuit occupied the remainder of the time after tea.

TITHE-RENT REDUCTION IN CHESHIRE. - The HOD. Howard Vyse has returned ten per cent. on the amounts due to him by his Cheshire tenantry) for the fourth time in suc- cession, in consequence of the losses farmers have sustained.

On VVednesday- the Duke of Westminster 'opened the Queen's School at Chestc-r, which has been established for the higher education of Rids in Cheshire, and which has been erected at a cost of £4,500 upon a site given by the Duke. It is expected that the school will be self-supporting. A supplement to the London Gazette, issued on Saturday night, contained tho official appointments of sheriffs for the year 1883, excepting Lancashire, Cornwall, and Middlesex. Mr. Arthur Hugh Smith Barry, of Marbury Hall, Northwicb, is appointed for Cheshire.

A: desperate :and diabolical attempt by a mother to burn her child was exposed in the Chester Police Court on Mon- day. A woman named Roberts, went home drunk, and, taking her child by the feet, flung it on the fire. Another 1 woman, named Antrobus, rescued the infant, but Roberts I again seized it and threw it on the fire. Antrobus again Isaved the child's life but the fiendish mother once more obtained possession Of it, and flung it upon the flames. Mrs. An trobus a third time rescued the child, and the mother finally attempted to throw akettle of boiling water upon her offspring. Mrs. Antrobus and the infant were severely scalded, and on being taken to the hospital the child's back was found to be fearfully burned.

div.head: PARTINGTON.
div.p: PARTINGTON.

A meeting in support of Mr. Latham's candidature was held in the Independent School-room, Partington, on Tues- day evening, and was presided over by Mr. G. F. Armitage. There was a good attendance. The CHAIRMAN, after explaining the object of the meet- ing, spoke strongly in favour of local option and a redis- tribution of seats, and enumerated the advantages that would accrue therefrom. He reminded those present that ief• absolutely secret so that the could fear- lessly record their votes tor tun unlu,.eeuua: ruvy Tr sou,. to elect. (Cheers.) Mr. WOODBURN, in speaking of the assimilation of the county and borough franchise, he said he believed brains to be before either capital or land, and he would go in for brains being represented. He impressed upon those present the advantages of the ballot. He said, without fear of contra- diction, that anyone could go into the polling booth and make his cross, and unless the voter chose to tell, nobody could get to know bow he had voted, not even the landlord if be paid a million of money. He did not be- lieve in religious toleration, but in religious equality. There was a great agitation for Sun- day closing, but apart from teetotalism as a social question, he would say that public-houses ought to be closed one day in seven. (Cheers.) But the Conservative candidate did not go in for that. If any of them believed in the sanctity of the Sabbath, he claimed their votes for the Liberal candidate. (Cheers.)

Mr. Porrs moved a resolution pledging the meeting to use all legitimate efforts to secure Mr. Latham's election. Mr. Latham had been engaged for many years in fighting the farmers' battle, and he had fought that battle amidst much obloquy. This election was a farmers' question, and he said, as a fellow farmer, that it would be an eternal disgrace to the farmers of Mid-Cheshire if they allowed Mr. Latham to be defeated. If they were to return Mr. Latham it would be a grand day for this country, for it would strike a key- note in every farming district in the kingdom. He believed every voter present had received a circular asking them to sly whether they would vote for Mr. Latham or Mr. Egerton. That was a gross piece of impertinence and in- timidation. Cheers.) He felt the utmost contempt for a person who would do such a thing. The farmers had no occasion to be afraid; they ought now to be able to turn the tables and make the landlords turn Liberal. They must not be intimidated; the ballot was absolutely secret. If the Tories would send coaveyances for them and insist upon them going, then let them go and have a ride out of them. He believed they would have a victory—. (cheers)—and no one would rejoice more than their great leader, Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) If they decided this battle in the right way it would-put" pluck and courage into the farmers throughout England, and they would be supporting a government which would give them those beneficial measures that the Conservative Government would not give them. If they sent Mr. Latham to Par liiment they would send a man who would be able to use a great influence towards getting those re'orms the farmers so much needed, tout if they did not send him it would, as ha had said before, ;be an eternal disgrace to _them. (Cheers.) _ _

Mr. Ntatorsox seconded the resolution. He said they had tried the Egertons several times, and he asked them to try Mr. Latham for once, and if they found he failed to do what they wished then they could go back to the Egertons acrain. But he did not think Mr. L'ltham would fail. If Mr. Latham went into Parliament he would most certainly go in for the farmer having compensation for his improve- ments. He did not know a man in the country who under- stood farming matters better than Mr. Latham did. Mr. Walker Mr. Swanwick, and Mr. Nicolls (Cheltenham) supported the resolution, which was put to the meeting and carried with only twodissentients, who were not voters. The meeting then terminated. - LYM M.
On Wednesday evening a meeting in support of Mr. Latham's candidature was held in the Jolly Thrasher, Lymm. Mr. H. Cameron presided, and there was a moderate attendance.

The CRAIRMAN said it seemed to Mtn that Mr. Egerton had come forward because he was the son of his father, or else that he was the brother of his brother. (Laugbter.) In Mr. Latham they had a gentleman who devoted a great deal of time and attention to the interests of the county, and he was well acquainted with the social as well as the political wants of the district. If they were fortunate enough to return him to Parliament they would have a member who would he able to carry out the desires of the Liberal party. But if they returned Mr. Egerton they would have an Egerton, a member of the Metropolitan Board of Works— (laughter)—and a man who would support such men as Lord Randolph Churchill, James Lowther, Ashmead-Bartlett, and company. (Laughter.) Mr. R A. NAYLOR moved a resolution that Mr. Latham is a fit and proper person to represent Mid-Cheshire in Parlia- ment, and pledging the meeting to do all in its power to secure his return. He spoke as a temperance politican, and as Mr. Latham was in favour of changing the licensing laws he would therefore give him his most hearty support. Mr. HOLT seconded the resolution. He, said that it had been repeatedly asserted that Mr. Egerton was a first-class landlord. (Hear, hear.) He thoroughly believed he was, but had he ever given the tenants more than they had a just rig,ht to demand? He had only dealt justly by them. But it was not a question whether Mr. Egerton had dealt justly by his tenants or not. What the farmers wanted was compensation for improvements, and if they wished to se- cure that they must vote for Mr. Latham. Professor A. S. W. Wrixix (Owens College), in a very able and interesting speech, defended the past and present policy of the Government. Other speakers followed, after which the re'solution WAS carried, and the meeting terminated: 1

SALE. Mr. G. W. Latham, the Liberal candidate, addressed g crowded gathering of electors at Sale,a suburb of Manchester, on Wednesday evening, and met with a cordial reception. He expressed his conviction that social as well as political re- forms were greatly needed. kr. Egerton had said he was a j director of two London hospitals, but he put it to them whether it would not be desirable that some effort should be made to carry reforms which would decrease the neces- sity for such hospitals by making our town populations more healthy, more thrifty, and more dependent upon their , own exertions. Land was never made to be accumulated by I, great men in masses. He would do nothing to prevent that ' accumulation, but he would do nothing to encourage it. The present laws are directly in favour of encouraging the accumulation and prohibiting the distribution. He would therefore vote for the abolition of the laws of entail and settle- ment, and the repeal of that absurd distinction in the devolu- tion of property between real property and peisonal property, so that the privileged olasses would not be able to accumulate land as they do now. Every man should have enough for his own comfort for his own share; but he would prevent, as far as he could, men by the aid of old, obsolete feudal laws accumulating land in masses when very often the owner was not in a position to make the most of the land. (Cheers.) Life was not so sweet in our large towns that they should not do their best to make it a little sweeter. Replyinc, to Mr. Egertoti's expression of doebt, fl-at, whether Mr. Latham had any property, and, second, suppos- ing he had any, whether he gave tenant right to his tenants, he said that if Mr. Egerton desired to be satisfied upon the points he would place in his hands one of his (Mr. Latham's) farming agreements on one condition, namely, that he would read it aloud at one of his meetings. (Load cheers.) 11 that was done they would see how the principle of compensation for improvements may be fairly and honestly dealt with. (Cheers.)

div.head: THELWALL.
div.p: THELWALL.

There was a moderate attendance at the meeting of the electors of the Grappenhall Polling District held in sup- port of Mr. Latham's candidature in the Temperance Hall, Thelrall, on Thursday evening. Mr. W. Darbyshire pre- sided, and was supported by Messrs. T. J. Cartwright, Matchant, Swanwick (Lymm), &c. The CHAIRMAN reminded the meeting that that was the third time Mr. Latham had solicited the suffrages of the electors, and he hoped, like the third time of asking in mar riage, it would be final, and that Mr. Latham would be elected member of Parliament for that division of the county. (Hear.) He supported Mr. Latham because he was in favour of giving compensation to tenant farmers for unexhausted manure and other improve- ments. It behoved the tenant farmers to get rid of everything that hindered them meeting foreign competition, and Mr. Latham, the candidate whom they wished to return to Parliament, will support a bill for pre- venting farmers' rents being raised upon their own improve- ments. He supported Mr. Latham also because he will support a bill for equalising the borough and county franchise, because he is in favour of abolishing the law of distraint, which was to him (the chairman) an abomination, and because Mr. Latham will give the people the right of saving how many public• houses they will have in their midst. Referring to the circular which had been sent by the Conservatives to the electors, he characterised it as the landlord screw being put on very nicely, considered it as forestalling the election and amounting to bribery and corruption, and remarked that it seemed to him an abominable thing to try to undermine the Ballot Act in such a way as was being tried by the Conserva- tives. (Cheers.) He urged them to support Mr. Latham, who he assured them was to be the winner. (Cheers.) Mr. CAwrwsitorrr moved a:resolution apwoving of Mr. Latham as a fit and proper person to represent Mid-Cheshire in Parliament. He said that in this election with the Con- servatives it was not the man but the name that was every- thing, while with the Liberals it was the reverse. Well he knew Mr. Latham, but he did not know Mr. Egerton; and he could assure them Mr. Latham was the most honest man they could possibly get to represent Mid-Cheshire in Par- liament. (Cheers.) He trusted they would vote for Mr. Latham, and try to secure a glorious victory for the Liberal cause on Wednesday ne-irt. (Cheer.) Mr. MARCHANT seconded the motion, and spoke in favour of an extension of the franchise, and maintained that the ballot was absolutely secret. The resolution was carried, and the meeting terminated with a vote of thanks to the chairman.
MR. EGERTON'S MEETINGS. MIDDLE WICH. LIVELY PROCEEDINGS.

A meeting in support of the Hon. Alan Egerton was held in the Town Hall, Middlewich, on Tuesday. The hall was occanied by about 250 persons, at least 150 of whom proved themselves during the meeting to be "on the other side." The chair was occupied by Lieutenant-Colonel C. H. France- Hayhurst. Mr. Egerton having addressed the meeting, chiefly defend- ing the circular which had been sent out to the electors, Mr. W. H. VERDIN proposed the following resolution That the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton is a fit and proper person to represent Mid-Cheshire in the House of Commons, and this meeting pledges itself to use all legitimate means to secure his election." He thought that after the very able address they had had from Mr. Egerton—(loud laugh- ter)—there were not many who had votes who would object to giving those votes for him on the day of the poll. Captain KENNEDY, who seconded the motion, was greeted with a fair share of derisive laughter during his rela'auplain UoTloe4, Cheshire, supported the resolution. The CHAIRMAN here asked if any one wished to ask the candidate a question, whereupon a gentleman from the body of the hall handed up a number of written questions, the answers to which caused much merriment.

Question No. 1 was: "Are you in favour of freedom of culture and sale of produce? Mr. EGERTON : Certainly, but with one condition, that is, the tenant places plenty of manure in proportion to what he takes away. Question No. 2.—" As you are not in favour of Sunday Closing, what measures will you support for the cure of drunkenness and its attendant evils pauperism and crime ? "

Mr. EGERTON (after a pause which caused some laugh ter). —That is a very wide question. (Loud laughter.) As to the question of drunkennesa, get a keeper; every man is his own keeper, and if you have that, the other two won't re- quire looking after—pauperism and crime. (Laughter.) Question No. 3.—" Ara you in favour of giving the work- ing man that is a householder in counties a vote ? "

-Mr. EGERTON : I said before, to every man—l think every man who has a stake in the country should have a vote. (Hear, hear.) Question No. 4.—" Will you support a measure giving compensation to farmers for damage done to crops and fences by foxhunters ?" (Loud cheers.) Mr. EGERTON : Here is a question that dces astonish me. I think that those who hunt bring a great deal of money into the country. Where wilful damage occurs, certainly those who do the wilful damage should pay for it. ("Hear, hear," and laughter.) Question No. 5 : "As an upholder of the Church and State, what section of the Church will you support ?" (Loud laughter.)
Mr. EdIiRTON : Why, the Church of England. (Renewed laughter.) __

-Question No. 6 : "Are you in favour of making compensation for unexhausted improvements compul- sory ? " Mr. EGERTON : If tenants can agree with their landlords —(hisses)—let them agree quickly. If they can't, why don't take the land. Let there be 'freedom of contract, but we don't want compulsion. (Hear, hear.) Are farmers of England children? (Laughter.) Do, they want a paternal Government to look after them? (Laughter.) They have a good deal more sense. (Hear, hear.) The farmer knows what he wants. If he can't get it in one county, well, get it in another.
Question No. 7 : "Has the salt tax in India been reduced by the present Government? If so, why don't you say so ?" (Laughter.)

• Mr. EGERTON : I don't know how to answer this question. (Laughter.) All I know is that the late Government started the reduction. (Hear, hear.) What I said was that it had not been abolished. The late Government made preparations in every way for its abolition. (Hear, bear.) Questh n No. 8: "If Mr. Egerton be elected, will be boldly meet the difficulty in the way of conscientious men entering Parliament by voting for the Affirmation Bill?" Mr. EGERTON : I should answer this by asking the writer another question. Who is the conscientious man? (A Voice : " Mr. Bradlaugh and all his followers." Cheers and counter cheers.) I would not own a conscience such as a gentleman who was indicted for indecent publications has. (Hear, hear.)_
Question No. 9: "Is Mr. Egerton in favour of perpetual pensions?"

Mr. EGERTON : No, I don't think I am, unless I get it my- self. ("Oh," and laughter.) This concluded the list of gnestions. Mr. EGERTON then rose to thank the meeting for their vote of confidence, when it dawned upon him that no such motion had been put. He resumed his seat amid much laughter, in which he himself joined. The CHAIRMAN put the resolution to the meeting, when about two-thirds—certainly more than one-half—voted against it.
-The CHAIRMAN caused more merriment by declaring the resolution carried by a !cage majority. The proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

At the Court-room, Halton Castle, on Monday evening, a meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Alan Egerton was held. Mr. Thomas Wright presided, and he was sup- ported by the Rev. J. Lockwood, Messrs. R. Pierpoint, J. W. Lightburn, Fisher, Somerville, T. Acton, and Jeacock. Several addresses were delivered, and a vote of confidence was passed.

ODD RODE. A meeting in support of the candidature of the Hon. de Tatton Egerton was held on Thursday at Odd Rode; Mr. Randle Wilbraham presided.—Mr. EGEnTorr, referring to the extension of the franchise, said that his remarks at Sand- tch upon this question had been misunderstood. When he spoke of representation pro rata be meant this—the hovering of the franchise would have to be accompanied by A redistribution of seats. He thought then that there should be one representative to a c,cgtain number of persons. He was in favour of giving a vote to all who were capable of using it,—A vote of centldence In the candidate was pawed.

RO fAL COLLEGE OF MUSIC, Kensington Gore, S.W., London. PRESIDENT: H. R. H. FRINGE OF WALES, E.G. Director: Hon. Secretary. GEORGE GROVE, ESQ., D.C.L. CHARLF.S MORLEY, ESQ. oTicE is HEREI3Y GivErt that the College will be opened in May, 1883, and that the Examinations, preliminary to the Final Competition for the first Fifty Open Scholarships, includ- ing Fifteen with Maintenance, will be held in Lohdon, aucl also Jo the principal Towns of the United Kingdom, on (or about) WEDNESDAY the 28th day of MARCH. Those Candidates only, who may be selected at these Pro- liminary Examinations, will be allowed to attend the Final Competition for Scholarships, before the Director and Board of Professors, at the College in London, in April next. Persons desiring to be admitted as Candidates for Scholar- ships must apply on Forms whch may be obtained at the Col- lege on application by letter or otherwise. The Forms must be returned so as to be received at the Office on or before the 19th day of March, 1883. The Prospectus of the College is nearly ready, and will be forwarded on application to the Honorary Secretary, Royal College of Music, Kensington Gore, S.W., London. The same advantages as are offered to scholars will be cpen, on certain terms and conditions, to paying Pupils (Students). The terms and conditions are stated in tua Prospectus. CHARLES MORLEY, Honorary Secretary. March, 1183.

Thirty-fourth Annual Report for theyear ending 31st December, 1882, The Directors have much pleasure in presenting their report and accounts for the year 1882. The reduction in the rate of expenditure in both branches has been continued during the year. The invested funds of the Company, including the paid- apeapital, now exceed three millions, viz., ordinary braneh, £928,176; industrial brateh. £2,119 223. ORDINARY BRANCH. The new business of this branch for the year consists of 7,067 policies, assuring the sum of £865,148, and producing a new annual premium income of £32,717. The claims of the year amount to £73,e21. representing 455 deaths and 24 endowment assurances matured. The annual premium income at the end of the year is £164,949, being an increase of £22,216 over the year 1881. Tz_e investments of the year have been made prin- cipally in consols, mortgages upon freehold property in London, and reversions. The rate of expenditure of the branch is less than ten and a-half percent on the premium income. . INDUSTRIAL BRANCA'. The Premiums actually received during the year In this branch are £2,126,022 35. llci. as competed with the sum of £1,849,494 18s. Id. received during 1681, being an increase of Premium Beet ipt.s of £276,827 ss. 6d. The claims of the year amount to £773,813, and the total amount of claims paid in this branch. is .21,559,925. The investments of the year have been made in New Three per Cents , Loans upon Rates, and Fteehold Ground Rents. The total expenses of this branch, as compared with those of the previous year, show a re- duction in the rate of expenditure of nearly two and a half per cent, on the premium inc •me. Alderman DAVIES, in reply to Councillor Mackie, said Sir John Rennie's report on the Mersey was handed to him by Lord Winmarleigh, and he had lent it whenever he thought by so doing he would promote the interests of Warrington.
